entries.title: Jordan Hicks raising his game in White Sox bullpen
entries.summary: <p>ARLINGTON, Texas — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> reliever Jordan Hicks is getting big results from a small tweak to his delivery that he made while recovering from the lat strain that kept him out of action for a month.</p><p>The hard-throwing right-hander raised his arm slot after “looking at some old video to try to replicate what worked in the past,” the veteran said, helping him find another tick on the 100 mph-plus fastball that put him on the map.</p><p>Hicks struck out two Rangers in his first outing since the All-Star break Monday, extending a 10-game scoreless streak since returning from the injured list June 21. Batters were 3-for-32 against him with 17 strikeouts over that stretch, lowering Hicks’ ERA nearly two full runs down to 3.62.</p><p>If his arm-slot fix sounds simple, Hicks credits another back-to-the-basics routine, too.</p><p>“I’ve also been playing catch more with my four-seam,” Hicks said. “That's what I was doing in ‘23,” when he struck out 81 hitters over 65⅔ innings with the Cardinals and Blue Jays. “With the four-seam, I always want to get a little more ride. That's why I like playing catch with it.”</p><h3><b>Colson nurses calf during laugher</b></h3><p>Colson Montgomery was out of the starting lineup Tuesday as the Sox laid a three-hit egg against Kumar Rocker and the Rangers. Noah Schultz served up five runs and couldn’t escape the fourth inning of a 10-0 loss — but infielder Luisangel Acuna pitched a perfect eighth frame of mop-up duty with a 38 mph curveball.</p><p>Montgomery sat after fouling a ball off his calf and exiting the series opener, but he’s “not worried about it being a long-term thing.”</p><p>“It was a direct hit on my calf muscle,” Montgomery said. “Completely missed my shin guard.”</p><p>Manager Will Venable said <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/20/colson-montgomery-all-star-snub-motivation" target="_blank" ><u>his slugging shortstop</u></a> was available off the bench and likely to start Wednesday.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> boating Mississippi River near his hometown of downstate Alton over the All-Star break, feasting on fish instead of hitters for one relaxing afternoon.</p><p>Not that it was all good eating. He and some friends were trolling for catfish but spent more time dodging Asian carp leaping out of water.</p><p>“They were literally jumping into the boat,” Hudson said of the invasive species. “Slimy, nasty guys.”</p><p>Hudson, who’s gone from floating around the waiver wire to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/14/alton-illinois-cubs-draft-pick-bryan-hudson-white-sox-cardinals-brewers" >anchoring the back of the Sox’ pen</a>, leapt out of the break with his latest nasty appearance in Toronto. He threw a flawless inning and a third in Sunday’s shutout win to lower his ERA on the season to 2.13 over 43 games.</p><p>“Chucking a few poles in the water is always nice,” the 6-8 reliever said, but he was itching to get back.</p><p>“In the break, it's always that's always on the back of your mind the whole time you're relaxing and whatnot — like, alright, still keep my body in shape, and mentally stay in shape as well to go out there and do it again in a few days,” Hudson said. “So to get that first one out of the way after the break is a good feeling.”</p><h3><b>Naperville Central star signs</b></h3><p>The Sox signed Naperville Central alumnus Colin Barczi as an undrafted free-agent catcher. He adds another local tie to the team’s newest crop of talent along with No. 34 pick <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/12/chicago-white-sox-mlb-draft-landon-thome-jim-thome-roch-cholowsky-andrew-benintendi-caleb-bonemer" >Landon Thome</a>, the Hall of Famer Jim’s son from Nazareth Academy, and Brother Rice grad Luke Lawrence, another infielder who went undrafted out of Kentucky.</p><p>Team scouts had projected Barczi as a third- to fifth-round pick out of Vanderbilt as he posted a .917 OPS in 31 games last season, until he went down with a shoulder injury.</p><p></p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Pete Crow-Armstrong wowing Cubs brass, who see walk as good as extra-base hit for speedy center fielder
entries.summary: <p>You might have heard that a walk can be as good as a hit.</p><p>But a walk being as good as a double?</p><p>Just another incredible baseball feat courtesy of <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b>.</p><p>“The ability to impact on the bases, you can’t pitch around him because it’s an extra-base hit. And if you pitch to him, it might be an extra-base hit,” team president <b>Jed Hoyer</b> said last week. “That’s the real beauty, he can get into scoring position so easily, and you can’t walk guys like that.”</p><p>For Crow-Armstrong, who’s wowing with his improved plate discipline, a walk can be as good as a double, as he can use his speed to easily swipe second base.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong — who started the day fifth in baseball with 25 stolen bases — flashed his speed in Tuesday’s 11-2 win over the Tigers, tripling in his first at-bat. That’s the kind of thing he did with regularity during his breakout 2025 campaign, establishing himself as a human highlight reel.</p><p>But in the same inning — the Cubs sent a dozen men to the plate in a six-run first — he showed what’s made him so newly dangerous this season, drawing a bases-loaded walk that forced in a run; he accounted for three of the team’s 11 walks on the night.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">PCA led off the first inning with a triple and now works a bases-loaded walk... it's still the first inning <a href="https://t.co/Bbt7YjJuui">pic.twitter.com/Bbt7YjJuui</a></p>— Talkin' Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) <a href="https://x.com/TalkinBaseball_/status/2079726491995103411?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 22, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>That’s the evolved PCA that shows the Cubs were onto something when they bet big with a $115 million contract extension.</p><p>“The way he’s played for the last six weeks or so is what you hoped he would get to eventually. He got there really quickly,” Hoyer said. “Obviously, he’s going to have to maintain it and stay there. But some of the great at-bats he’s had?</p><p>“He was facing [lefty reliever <b>Sam] Moll</b> with Cincinnati, and I found myself thinking, ‘Oh, he’s going to walk him.’ And I was like, ‘Wow, that is a 180.’ I never would have thought that last year, that he was going to face that kind of guy … and he’s not going to chase a breaking ball away, he’s going to have a disciplined approach. He’s kind of impossible [to pitch to] when you get to that place.</p><p>“This current approach is exactly what we always hoped he could get to. It just came a lot faster than we thought.”</p><p>He’s doing incredible things with his glove, too, turning in another highlight-reel grab Tuesday.</p><p>“They’re plays that nobody else is going to make,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “You’re going to have to watch baseball a long time to find somebody who’s going to make the plays. That’s how good it is.”</p><h3><b>Shaw still waiting to swing</b></h3><p>The Cubs are still waiting for utility man <b>Matt Shaw</b> to be entirely free of the symptoms caused by the sprained hand that’s had him sidelined since late last month.</p><p>Counsell touted improvement for Shaw on Tuesday, but despite new imaging showing “significant healing,” Shaw is still waiting to start swinging a bat.</p><p>“We’ve just got to get over that last step. It’s been a stubborn sprain, so to speak. But he’s improving,” Counsell said. “When you swing a baseball bat for a living, it involves the wrist heavily, and we’re just not quite past it.”</p><p>Shaw will head to Arizona to continue working when the Cubs next hit the road.</p><h3><b>Party like it’s 1999</b></h3><p>With his two-run blast Tuesday, <b>Michael Conforto</b> became the second Cub since at least 1901 to hit four pinch-hit homers in a season, matching <b>Glenallen Hill</b>’s franchise record from 1999.</p><p>It was the latest contribution from Conforto, who has carved out a nice role as a part-timer, owning an .824 OPS that’s his best since 2020.</p><p>“It’s always, ‘Can you find a player that can do this job and be successful at it?’” Counsell said. “Michael has done a fabulous job at it, and you feel like it’s a real weapon to have somebody like that.”</p><h3><b>Climbing the list</b></h3><p>Left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b>’s home run Monday was the 191st of his career and sent him into sole possession of 11th place on the Cubs’ all-time home-run list, passing Hall of Fame outfielder <b>Hack Wilson</b>.</p><p>He’s seven away from tying MVP outfielder <b>Hank Sauer</b>, who’s currently 10th with 198 home runs as a Cub.</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: Bring this cochinita pibil recipe to your next family dinner
entries.summary: <p>Brothers and restaurateurs Teddy and Alexis Vejar spent their childhood surrounded by great cooks both in Mexico and the US. Of all the dishes they grew up eating, one remains their favorite all these years later: cochinita pibil. Now, they run the restaurant Jarabe on the city’s Near West Side, where they serve cochinita pibil.</p><h2><b>Cochinita Pibil</b></h2><p><i>Yields: 1 oz · 1.0 plate of 1 oz</i></p><p><b>INGREDIENTS</b></p><p>5 lb Pork Butt- Bone In</p><p>1.5 cup Recado Rojo</p><p>1 piece White Onions</p><p>4 piece Banana Leaves</p><p>2 tbsp Kosher Salt</p><p>1 oz Bay Leaves</p><p></p><p><b>METHOD</b></p><p></p><p>1. Trim only any loose pieces of fat or skin from the pork butt. Leave the majority of the fat cap intact, as it helps keep the meat moist during the long cook. Pat the pork dry with paper towels and salt.</p><p></p><p>2. Coat the Pork with the achiote paste making sure it covers every surface.</p><p></p><p>NOTE Preferably at this step transfer pork to a non reactive container and leave marinating in the fridge for 6-12 Hours.</p><p></p><p>3. If using frozen banana leaves, thaw them completely and run over a flame to soften.</p><p></p><p>4. Line Roasting pan with Banana leaves and add pork and achiote mixture.</p><p></p><p>5. Slice 1 whole white onion and top the pork with the onion slices.</p><p></p><p>6. Add Bay leaf to the roasting pan and cover with remaining banana Leaves.</p><p></p><p>7. Cover pan with foil</p><p></p><p>8. Pre Heat oven to 225 Degrees</p><p></p><p>9. Place Roasting pan in the middle rack of the oven and cook 8-10 hours or until the bone pull out cleanly.</p><p></p><p>10. Unwrap banana leaves and remove Pork from cooking liquid</p><p></p><p>11. Strain cooking liquid to remove any grainy spices.</p><p></p><p>12. Add Cooking liquid to a sauce pan and reduce until it becomes slightly thickened about 15–25 minutes.</p><p></p><p>13. Transfer the pork to a serving container, shred and cover with the reduced cooking liquid</p><p></p><p>NOTE Serve with warm corn tortillas, pickled red onions and minced habanero peppers.</p><p></p><h2><b>Recado Rojo</b></h2><p><i>Yields: 5 lb</i></p><p><b>INGREDIENTS</b><br>10 oz Annato Ground<br>2 oz Mexican Oregano<br>2 oz Cinnamon Mexican<br>2 oz Corriander<br>2 oz Cumin Whole<br>2 oz All Spice<br>1 oz Cloves<br>1 oz Black Pepper Ground<br>16 oz Ajo/ Garlic<br>1 qt Guajillo Puree<br>16 oz Distilled White Vinegar<br>32 oz Orange Juice<br>32 oz Lime Juice<br>1 oz Kosher Salt</p><p><b>METHOD</b><br>1. In a dry skillet or cast iron pan over medium heat, toast the cumin. Cook for 2–3 minutes, stirring constantly, until fragrant. Allow to cool slightly.</p><p>2. Measure and weigh all spices and combine.</p><p>3. Add to a high-powered blender: garlic, orange juice, lime Juice, vinegar, guajillo purée and blend until completely smooth.</p><p>4 Add: Ground annatto, Mexican oregano, ground cinnamon, ground coriander, toasted cumin, ground allspice, ground cloves, ground black pepper and Kosher salt. Blend on high until the paste is completely smooth. If necessary, scrape down the sides and blend again.</p><p>5 . The finished achiote paste should be thick but pourable. If it's too thick, add a little more orange juice. If it's too thin, blend in additional annatto powder, a tablespoon at a time.</p><p>6. Transfer to a food-safe container and refrigerate overnight. This allows the spices to fully hydrate</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Boyfriend's TikTok following gives her cause for concern
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I recently started dating a guy I have known for 30 years. He has moved in and asked me to marry him. Our relationship is perfect except for anything having to do with social media. He has an account on TikTok using a sexually suggestive name.</p><p>He's following 500 women and has just as many following him. I'm worried this will lead to other things, and the fact that he hides this from me makes it worse. Of all the women he follows, I am not on his list, and that hurts, too. I'm sure other readers deal with this issue, and I'm not sure how to handle this situation. Is this a form of cheating, or, because it is social media, should I not worry about it?</p><p>To my knowledge, he doesn't chat with any of them, or maybe he has that hidden so I don't see it and will probably never know for sure. Should I end this relationship because of doubt — which I'm worried will turn into trust issues — or shrug it off? — <i>UNCERTAIN IN SOUTH CAROLINA</i></p><p><b>DEAR UNCERTAIN:</b> How does your partner earn his living? Following 500 women seems time-consuming. If he's hiding it from you, how do you know this? Your doubt, which is reasonable, already is a trust issue.</p><p>I will assume that you know about his "hobby" because you looked at his computer or phone. If you felt the need to do that, do not shrug it off. Have a heart-to-heart talk with him and ask what he's seeking from these online relationships. Is he a voyeur or looking for adventure? Once you know the answer to those questions, you will know how to proceed.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My mother is 86 years old. She has been widowed for more than 10 years. She works, sings in a choir, volunteers at her church and has three children who dote on her, but she desperately wants a man in her life — and the man she wants is married. They have been together for more than five years on and off. They get together, feel guilty and break up. This has happened more than 20 times.</p><p>She lies to us, her counselor and her friends about this affair. We are tired of her lies, her crying over the adulterer and her inability to enjoy what she has instead of complaining about what she doesn't have. Doctors, counselors and church members have all tried to convince her this pattern is destructive, to no avail. Help! — <i>OVER IT</i></p><p><b>DEAR OVER IT:</b> It sounds like Mom may be in love with the drama more than the man. The best way to deal with it would be to stop engaging. When she starts discussing her affair, change the subject. If she persists, leave the room. Let her know that you really are "over it." Tell her you refuse to watch her make a fool of herself any longer. Then encourage her to talk about the parts of her life that are not so self-destructive.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>For an excellent guide to becoming a better conversationalist and a more sociable person, order "How to Be Popular." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Popularity Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Time to take charge: Bears QB Caleb Williams must be so on top of his job that he can keep others on track
entries.summary: <p>True leadership grows organically, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> hope quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a> is ready to fully step into that role when they open training camp Wednesday.</p><p>It can’t be forced, as it was when Williams was a rookie and the team wanted him to run the show on a roster stocked with veterans. It can’t be rushed, either, as it was a year ago when Williams could barely stay afloat while trying to learn coach Ben Johnson’s offense, let alone worry about what anyone else was doing.</p><p>Training camp was such a nightmare — Johnson was all over him starting with his huddle command and pre-snap process — that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/12/23/first-impression-bears-caleb-williams-ben-johnson-mesh-after-rocky-start" >Williams questioned whether his coach liked him</a>. Williams said last month he expected camp would be “a hell of a lot more fun for me” this year now that he’s in sync with Johnson.</p><p>“I feel like I was drowning,” he said of last summer.</p><p>There’s been a lot of talk from the Bears, including directly from Williams and Johnson, over the last few months about how far ahead the team will be compared to this time last year, but it’s just talk until there’s proof. If it’s true, it’ll be evident with a smooth start to camp.</p><p>Williams is going into Year 3, and even accounting for all the turbulence he weathered as a rookie, this is roughly the time when most great quarterbacks find their way.</p><p>It shouldn’t take weeks or months for him to hit his stride. Everything Williams does should look and sound right, from the huddle through the end of the play. And he needs to be so on top of his own responsibilities that he has the bandwidth to keep teammates on track as an extension of Johnson.</p><p>“That's a part of growth,” he said. “You don't just get [that authority] just because of the position. You’ve got to work hard, you’ve got to grow and you’ve got to win.</p><p>“Be the same guy every day. Come in here and work. Do all the things right that I'm supposed to do. If there's extra that I need to do — if it's sitting down and talking to them, if it's on the field and you’ve got to yell and get them back to the huddle, or any of those little things. It's whatever it takes to get to the end goal.”</p><p>Johnson said Williams being able to run the team as a pseudo-coach, “comes with the comfort level in terms of knowing what’s being asked of the offense.” He saw improvement in that area during Organized Team Activities and minicamp and said Williams “certainly is a vocal presence within our offense and our entire team.”</p><p>Williams earned a lot of credibility with teammates last season by leading the Bears to seven fourth-quarter comebacks, including one in the playoffs. That also made him one of the NFL’s most popular players. And it helped that Johnson, while still critical, backed him emphatically.</p><p>But Madden covers and other accolades will melt away when camp starts. Johnson won’t care about any of that if the offense is clunky and Williams hasn’t spent his offseason fixing some of the flaws that have held him back the last two seasons.</p><p>In all the excitement over Williams — When was the last time there was this big of a groundswell, both locally and nationally, behind a Bears quarterback? — it could be easy to lose sight of how much work he still must do.</p><p>The fanbase doesn’t seem to want to hear any criticism of Williams at the moment, but Johnson doesn’t have any aversion to it. Both things can be true simultaneously: He’s exciting player with a bright future and he’s still got a long way to go.</p><p>Johnson loves Williams’ improvisational skills, but he’s far too precise and calculated of a tactician to have his quarterback play the whole game like that. Johnson enjoyed the heroics, but said consistently he didn’t think that was a sustainable formula.</p><p>It wouldn’t have taken much for some of those victories to flip to losses, and Williams would be viewed much differently if, perhaps, three games had gone the other way. That’s the warning heading into this season.</p><p>Johnson has his eye on Williams’ completion percentage, which was a league-low 58.1 among players who threw at least 250 passes. If that feels like nitpicking after a season in which he set the franchise record for yards passing (3,942) and led the Bears to their first playoff win in 15 years, take it up with the coach.</p><p>Johnson set the bar at 70% a year ago and said that standard applied not only to season but to every day of training camp and practice. Williams never hit that mark in a game.</p><p>It’s not a definitive statistic, but it’s vital to the efficiency Johnson wants to see in the passing attack. Raising his completion percentage also would reflect that Williams has fully adopted what Johnson and quarterbacks coach J.T. Barrett have been teaching him about footwork and timing.</p><p>Williams’ first two years were wild. His season with former coach Matt Eberflus was dysfunctional across the board and he got sacked like crazy, and things didn’t click between him and Johnson, in Williams’ mind, until November. This is the time for him to level out as a player and take control as a leader, and those goals are inextricable from each other.</p>

entries.title: Ancient city's demise point to dangers of climate change
entries.summary: <p>The smoke came down out of Canada last week. It turned the skies in Chicago and throughout the Midwest the color of dishwater. Then it kept coming south, until it drifted over a field across the river from St. Louis where the largest city north of what is now Mexico once stood.</p><p>Most of us were never taught it was there.</p><p>A thousand years ago, 10,000 to 20,000 people lived at Cahokia. They farmed corn on the bottomland, traded copper down from the Great Lakes and shell up from the Gulf, and raised 120 mounds of packed earth one basket at a time, the largest a 100 feet high and fourteen acres at its base.</p><p>It was bigger than London. It was a city.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-0c0000" name="module-0c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>I have stood on top of them. You climb, and the ground keeps rising longer than you expect, and at the top the whole valley lies open underneath you, and eight miles west the St. Louis skyline stands up out of it. It is quiet up there. Grass and wind, and nothing at all to tell you what you are standing on. You have to be told. Then you look again, and the field is not a field anymore.</p><p>Cahokia rose in good years. Tree rings say it was founded during one of the wettest 50-year stretches of the millennium, when the rain came on time and the bottomland gave back everything it was asked for.</p><p>Then the rains changed. Drought came after 1150. Around 1200, a flood big enough to swallow the farmland left its signature in the mud of a lake beside the city.</p><p>We can watch what happened next. They left it in the ground.</p><p>Around 1175, the Cahokians put a wall around the heart of their city, two miles of it, 20,000 logs sunk in trenches five feet deep, with towers every 85 feet, the spacing a man needs to cover his neighbor with a bow.</p><p>They built that wall four times. Each time, they used fewer logs. There were fewer hands left to carry them.</p><p>Walls like it went up across the middle of the continent between 1200 and 1400. In a cemetery in the Illinois River valley, dating to about 1300, at least a third of the adults died violently. Scalped. Shot. Left where they fell. Farther up the Missouri, at a place called Crow Creek, a village dug a ditch and raised a wall to keep itself safe, and around 1325 at least 486 of its people were killed and buried in it, their bones showing they had been hungry long before anyone came.</p><p>That was not Cahokia. Different people, different place. And no honest scholar will tell you the drought pulled the trigger.</p><p>But that is what hunger and fear look like when they last long enough. Why Cahokia emptied is still argued. And the story I was taught turns out to be false. It said the Cahokians cut down too many trees and flooded themselves out. Archaeologists went looking for that flood and could not find it. It had never been tested. It was only believed, because it flattered us to believe it.</p><p>The likelier answer is harder. The climate changed first. Then the pressures came together. The harvests got thin. The politics got mean. The trust wore out. Some families left, then more, and by 1400 the plazas were empty and the grass had come back over them.</p><p>That is the order of it. Climate change starts in the sky and the soil. Then it moves through food, fear, power and faith.</p><p>Columbus did not reach the Caribbean until 1492. He never saw Cahokia.</p><p>Here is what those mounds say to me.</p><p>They say a people can build something so large a thousand years of weather cannot erase it.</p><p>They say the same people can be pressed until they wall themselves off from one another.</p><p>They say a people can walk away from all of it, and regather, and build again.</p><p>They say all three things. They are the same mounds. Cahokia’s people did not vanish. They walked. They regathered. They built again. Andrea Hunter, who keeps the history of the Osage Nation, will tell you her people trace their ancestry to that world and are still here, in Oklahoma.</p><p>That is the hope. It is not a promise.</p><p>Last week the smoke drifted over the city you can see from up there, and over the city you are standing on.</p><p>Two things are still in that ground. The mounds they raised together. The trenches they dug when the trust ran out.</p><p>We are building both right now.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p>
entries.author: Ben Jealous

entries.title: Never underestimate value of Medicare
entries.summary: <p>As we celebrate another anniversary of Medicare and Medicaid this month, I'm reminded how quickly life can change — and how important these programs are for people facing unexpected health challenges.</p><p>For years, I traveled the world as a federal regulatory affairs professional, conducting inspections of clinical research trials and pharmaceutical facilities. I loved my work, the people I met and the sense of purpose it gave me.</p><p>Then I was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis.</p><p>As my condition progressed, I could no longer travel and eventually had to retire on disability. Losing my career meant losing much of the independence I had worked so hard to build. Thankfully, qualifying for Medicare through Social Security Disability gave me access to the healthcare I need, including monthly infusion treatments that help me manage my disease.</p><p>Recently, Medicare protected me in another unexpected way.</p><p>While walking with my granddaughter after getting ice cream, we were struck by a car while crossing the street. We were both taken to the emergency room in separate ambulances. The accident was traumatic enough without worrying about how I would pay for emergency medical care.</p><p>Because I have Medicare, I could focus on healing instead of facing overwhelming medical bills.</p><p>Too often, we don't appreciate programs like Medicare until we need them. For me, Medicare has meant peace of mind through chronic illness, disability and an unexpected emergency. It has allowed me to focus on my health instead of financial hardship.</p><p>As Medicare and Medicaid mark another year of serving Americans, I hope we remember that these programs aren't just benefits — they're lifelines. We must protect them so that everyone can receive the care they need when life takes an unexpected turn.</p><p><i>Lequita Michelle Mayhew, Bronzeville </i></p><h3>Both political parties rightfully ‘hate Illinois Nazis’ </h3><p>Most political disagreements are healthy.</p><p>What should never be up for debate is whether hatred, racism, antisemitism, and political extremism deserve a place in our public life.</p><p>That is why I found it refreshing to see both major political parties filed objections to remove Richard “Sieg Heil” Mayers from the November ballot after he attempted to run for statewide office under the banner of the “Germanic Aryan Supremacy Smokers, Gamblers” party. Mayers has a history of promoting white supremacist and antisemitic rhetoric.</p><p>The Democratic Party condemned the hate he represents. The Republican Party did the same.</p><p>Good. They should. Everyone should.</p><p>We all understand that the disagreement between conservatives and liberals is not the same as the disagreement between democracy and extremism. One side may favor lower taxes. The other may favor increased public investment. One side may advocate for stronger regulation. The other may push for market-based solutions.</p><p>Those are legitimate political debates. Nazism is not. White supremacy is not. Antisemitism is not.</p><p>Many Illinoisans remember the embarrassment surrounding Arthur Jones, the Holocaust denier who became a Republican nominee for Congress in 2018 after running unopposed in a primary. Republicans attempted to distance themselves from him. Democrats used his candidacy as evidence of broader problems within the Republican Party. The controversy consumed attention that could have been spent discussing actual policy and actual solutions.</p><p>The result was predictable. Extremism benefited from publicity while the public’s trust in politics suffered.</p><p>This time, both parties appear determined not to repeat that mistake.</p><p>Going through the objections filed against Mayers, I could not help but think of one of the most memorable lines from The Blues Brothers: “I hate Illinois Nazis.”</p><p>The line is funny because it is absurd. Yet beneath the humor lies a truth that remains relevant decades later.</p><p>The principles of human dignity, religious freedom, equal protection under the law and respect for our fellow citizens are values worth defending.</p><p>These are not Democratic values or Republican values. They are American values, and knocking Mayers off the ballot was the right move.</p><p><i>James M. Vasselli, Hinsdale</i></p><h3>More info, please, about corrections to assessments</h3><h3></h3><p>Your property tax bill depends on more than market values — it depends on the accuracy of the property data used to calculate those values.</p><p>Cook County has a long-standing systemic property data governance problem. Audits have identified it, the assessor's office has documented it, and the incoming assessor made improving property data a central campaign issue. Yet Illinois law does not require a transparent interagency governance and public reporting framework to measure whether verified factual property data errors identified during the appeals process are consistently shared, corrected and incorporated into the official assessment records.</p><p>Good governance requires more than correcting errors — it requires transparency, accountability and measurable results. Taxpayers and policymakers should be able to see how many verified property data errors are identified, how many are corrected and whether the system is improving over time.</p><p>Illinois should require a formal governance and reporting framework that ensures verified factual property data corrections become part of the official record and are publicly measured.</p><p>Property tax fairness begins with accurate data, but it ultimately depends on equity, transparency and governance.</p><p><i>Tony Bonvolanta, North Center</i></p><h3>Global warming crises are here</h3><h3></h3><p>Fifty years ago, scientists and visionaries warned us of the impact of global warming. The skeptics said we wouldn't do anything until we had a crisis! Well, guess what?</p><p><i>Tim Ressel, Glen Ellyn</i><br></p>

entries.title: States — and Justice Department — should resist bad old days of warehousing people with disabilities
entries.summary: <p>For three years, Stanley has lived in her own apartment on Chicago's South Side. She cooks her own meals, sees her family regularly and manages her bipolar disorder with the kind of stability that once felt impossible. Previously, her only option besides living on the street was a nursing home — a place she describes not as somewhere to heal, but somewhere to survive.</p><p>It was a place that didn't feel safe, and where Stanley, whose last name is being withheld to protect her privacy, felt like the residents and employees were working against her and her recovery.</p><p>Stanley’s path to recovery and independence was made possible by the little-known <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/supct/html/98-536.ZS.html" target="_blank" >Olmstead</a> integration mandate, born from a 1999 Supreme Court ruling that found unjustified institutionalization of people with disabilities is discrimination. Since that decision, this principle has pushed states to treat people in their communities, rather than hide them in institutions.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-260000" name="module-260000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>As community mental health practitioners with more than 40 years of experience, we have witnessed how deinstitutionalization transformed care in Illinois and the lives of each individual given the opportunity to thrive and determine their own future.</p><p>It's why Thresholds — which provides community-based behavioral health and supportive housing across the Chicago area — has helped thousands of people move out of nursing homes and psychiatric facilities, and into successful, supportive living situations.</p><p>Jan Wrightsell was the first person Thresholds helped move. After years in and out of hospitals for schizophrenia, depression and psychosis, she left a nursing home in 2010 for her own apartment in Hyde Park. She never thought she'd be able to live on her own, but thanks to the community-based support made possible through Olmstead-related settlements in Illinois, she returned to her community and started her recovery journey.</p><p>Sixteen years later, she’s a working artist and a longtime peer support facilitator who shares her story to help others find their way, too.</p><h3>DOJ narrows view of law</h3><h3></h3><p>Last month, the U.S. Department of Justice <a class="Link" href="https://www.justice.gov/olc/media/1446701/dl" target="_blank" >released a memo</a> espousing a dramatically narrower interpretation of federal disability law. The DOJ concluded that the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Rehabilitation Act don't actually obligate states to serve people with mental illness in the community — a much narrower interpretation than nearly every federal court has taken of Olmstead.</p><p>The memo doesn't change the law or existing consent decrees, but it signals the DOJ may stop enforcing them, opening the door for states to roll back community-based care.</p><p>This is the difference between living in your own home with a say in your own life and being locked away. Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy warned in his Olmstead<i> </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/supct/pdf/98-536P.ZC1" target="_blank" >concurrence</a> in 1999 about the risk of pushing people out of care too fast and with too little support. That's a legitimate concern that deserves real investment, but it's not an excuse to abandon the commitment to community integration.</p><p>Institutional care is a part of the continuum of care for those with very high needs beyond a hospital inpatient stay. But that care must be focused on supporting the client’s recovery to become well enough to move back to the least restrictive environment possible.</p><p>Recent federal actions also reinforce longstanding misconceptions linking people experiencing homelessness and mental illness to crime, but they are <a class="Link" href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24672998/" target="_blank" >far more likely</a> to be victims of crime than to victimize others. Public policy should be guided by evidence and experience, not stigma or misconceptions.</p><h3>Housing, paired with clinical support, works</h3><h3></h3><p>What the evidence does<i> </i>support is what Thresholds has done for six decades: Pair stable housing with real clinical support. Our work is proven both clinically and financially. Most people we've helped move out of institutions have stayed out, and a housing voucher plus our highest level of community care costs taxpayers less than a nursing home placement.</p><p>This isn't a choice between compassion and fiscal responsibility. The evidence demonstrates that community-based care advances both.</p><p>We understand the impulse behind these efforts. Cities are struggling visibly with homelessness and untreated mental illness, and institutions can look like a clean solution. They are not. People living with mental illness are not a problem to be managed out of view. They are our neighbors. Our family. Our co-workers. Our friends.</p><p>Stanley and Jan’s stability isn't a fluke. They are the result of a system built, slowly and deliberately, on the idea that people with mental illness deserve to live in their communities, not apart from them. Congress and state leaders should reject the DOJ's invitation to retreat from that promise.</p><p>We cannot go back to the dark days of unnecessary institutionalization, not when we know, and have proven, that there's a better way.</p><p><i>Peggy Flaherty and Debra Howard-Frye are co-chief clinical officers at Thresholds, a nonprofit organization that provides housing, employment and recovery services for people with mental illness and substance use disorders in Illinois.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-000000" name="module-000000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Rainbow Cone marks 100th anniversary serving up its signature sliced and stacked treat
entries.summary: <p>To the uninitiated, a Rainbow Cone with its five colorful ice creams stacked in a seemingly gravity-defying way might seem like a recent Instagram-inspired creation. But Chicagoans, especially those on the South Side, know that the Original Rainbow Cone shop and its photogenic namesake are local institutions that predate social media — along with cellphones, computers, the first fully electronic television, microwaves and a host of other modern-day conveniences.</p><p>Launched in August 1926 in a small shack at 92nd Street and Western Avenue, Rainbow Cone turns 100 this year with a slew of events (see below) to mark the celebration. Activities around the city include an immersive experience at the Museum of Ice Cream Chicago and pop-ups at Lookingglass Theatre and Lurie Children’s Hospital.</p><p>Back when Joe and Katherine Sapp started the business, Beverly was nothing like it is today. The couple saw potential in the area that was dominated by dirt roads and dotted with apple orchards and summer cottages. A cemetery across the street proved to be beneficial. </p><p>“Sunday was their biggest day of the week,” said Lynn Sapp, who was the third-generation owner of Rainbow Cone. “People would go to the cemetery to visit loved ones, and they would stop at Rainbow on their way back to the city.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A car mechanic by trade, Joe was inspired to open Rainbow Cone for a simple reason. “He always loved ice cream and was fascinated by it,” said Sapp. The five flavors of the cone, originally 12 cents, were a nod to the popularity of the era’s three-flavor Neapolitan ice cream.</p><p>Rather than scoops, the Rainbow Cone’s ice creams were sliced into slabs using a special tool Joe created, a clever eye-catching design element that also helped hold it together. The ice creams’ order is the same now as it was then: chocolate, strawberry, Palmer House (vanilla with walnuts and cherries), pistachio and orange sherbet on top.</p><p>Not too long after Rainbow Cone opened, the Depression started. Sapp credits her grandmother with keeping the business afloat. “Katherine was the businesswoman behind him and threw her nickel around like a sewer cover,” she said, adding that her grandfather was “a genius of a man who could fix anything.”</p><p>Joe’s handiwork could be seen all over Rainbow Cone, especially when it moved across the street to a larger location where the couple lived on the second floor of the two-story building painted pink, Katherine’s favorite color. There was a mechanical bird he made that would tell customers to move down the line. It didn’t last long as everybody would stop to look at the bird and no one would move.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f00000" name="image-f00000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7f143b3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8a%2Fad%2Fe6eb13e04107ac0d66fa86a20710%2Frainbowcone-260722-7.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7e5d882/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8a%2Fad%2Fe6eb13e04107ac0d66fa86a20710%2Frainbowcone-260722-7.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7750400/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8a%2Fad%2Fe6eb13e04107ac0d66fa86a20710%2Frainbowcone-260722-7.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Lynn Sapp constructs the namesake Rainbow Cone inside the business’ founding location at 9233 S. Western Ave. in the Beverly neighborhood." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7750400/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8a%2Fad%2Fe6eb13e04107ac0d66fa86a20710%2Frainbowcone-260722-7.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/723ee35/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8a%2Fad%2Fe6eb13e04107ac0d66fa86a20710%2Frainbowcone-260722-7.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7750400/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8a%2Fad%2Fe6eb13e04107ac0d66fa86a20710%2Frainbowcone-260722-7.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Lynn Sapp constructs the namesake Rainbow Cone at the Beverly shop. “When it’s a family business, it’s at your dinner table and you live with it,” said Sapp, who started working at Rainbow Cone’s counter when she was 14 years old. Her three older siblings worked there, too.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The mirrors at 92nd are the same mirrors as when Rainbow Cone opened 100 years ago, Sapp says. “It was Al Capone days. The gangsters were alive and well. So, the way the parlor was designed, [her grandfather] put up mirrors all everywhere. He could stand anywhere in the store and by looking in a mirror, he knew exactly who was coming in.”</p><p>During World War II, a shortwave radio Joe built drew in customers with cones in hand to the shop’s back patio eager for updates. “It became an information center for the neighborhood,” Sapp said.</p><p>In the ’60s, Sapp’s parents, Robert and Jean, who lived in a house behind Rainbow Cone, took over the business. Growing up, Sapp, like her three older siblings, worked there. “When it’s a family business, it’s at your dinner table and you live with it,” said Sapp, who started working at Rainbow Cone’s counter when she was 14, calling it “an honor and a privilege” despite the long days and hard work.</p><p>“When you’d hear people's stories like, ‘Oh my gosh, I came here with my grandparents and I haven't had this in 10 years and it brings back such memories,’ that really helps.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The Rainbow Cone layers are and always have been, from bottom to top of the cone: chocolate, strawberry, Palmer House (vanilla with walnuts and cherries), pistachio and orange sherbet.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>It also didn’t hurt living behind an ice cream parlor. “We always had ice cream all around us,” she said.</p><p>While her siblings went on to careers in other fields, Sapp stayed on and took over the business in 1987. First order of business was doing away with the fancy white outfits the staff wore, typical of ice cream parlors back then, and swapping in T-shirts.</p><p>Rainbow’s menu had been through some changes, growing and contracting over the years. Sapp put some items back — think sundaes, shakes and floats — and added her own: ice cream cakes and rolls. Pints and quarts followed. The Rainbow Cone’s ice cream recipes, however, stayed the same beyond changes due to new health regulations, such as the pasteurization of nuts. And the namesake Rainbow Cone is still the top seller.</p><p>One element of her role that Sapp particularly liked was working with the young staff. “It was part of my mission to send them out into the world where they could produce and contribute and make a good living,” she said. “I used to joke with them that if you’re having difficulties with an ice cream cone, you’ve got a problem.”</p><p>Bryan Feltman started working behind the ice cream counter when he was 16 years old. Seventeen years later, he’s still there, albeit now he’s a managing partner. In addition to helping oversee stores, he heads up Rainbow Cone pop-ups like at Taste of Chicago, Lollapalooza and local street fairs.</p><p>“I always knew Rainbow was more than an ice cream shop,” said Feltman, who grew up in Beverly going there as a kid as did his dad. “It’s been passed down from one generation to the next and has become a tradition for birthday parties, home run celebrations, first dates and so many other things. There are a lot of memories and emotions attached to this brand.”</p><p>Feltman has also been on the frontlines dealing with customers who might be hesitant to try the unique ice cream combo. “It’s five flavors that are great on their own but together there’s just something magical about it,” he said. Rainbow Cone offers customers a replacement menu item if they’re not satisfied, but Feltman can count on one hand the number of times he’s had to do that. “It has stood the test of time for 100 years and that alone speaks volumes.”</p><p>After years in the business, Sapp began thinking about winding down her involvement in the company. She also recognized the need to find a company that could embrace technology at Rainbow Cone in a way she wasn’t able to. “The goal was getting as many people to know Rainbow Cone as possible because I think it’s a very unique product, and I’m very proud of it,” she said. </p><p>With no family members interested, she reached out to a neighboring Beverly company, Buona Beef, a multigenerational restaurant chain specializing in Italian beef.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5c0000" " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/046789d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F68%2Fb3%2F500513c44efcaacdc37b842dcc1f%2Frainbowconetruck-07032024-3.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e6b48f1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F68%2Fb3%2F500513c44efcaacdc37b842dcc1f%2Frainbowconetruck-07032024-3.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/046789d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F68%2Fb3%2F500513c44efcaacdc37b842dcc1f%2Frainbowconetruck-07032024-3.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The Rainbow Cone ice cream truck was born during Covid, when restaurants as well as the seasonal festivals were shut down. Johnny Buonavolanto’s cousin came up with the idea of an ice cream truck. They painted an old FedEx truck bright pink with white polka dots and brought it to their Buona Beef parking lots. “We had lines down the block and wrapped around the streets,” said Buonavolanto, director of sales for the Buona Companies.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“She had bigger companies interested but she wanted a Chicago family-owned business to take care of this brand, be a steward of it and honor her family’s legacy,” said Johnny Buonavolanto, director of sales for the Buona Companies. That company was started in 1981 by his grandfather, who, at 90 years old, still comes to the office.</p><p>Since Buona came on board as owners in 2018, Rainbow Cone has grown from two locations (Beverly and Navy Pier) to 30, including ones inside Buona Beef restaurants and in states outside Illinois. Buonavolanto assured Rainbow Cone fans that Sapp is still very much a part of the company and consults on key decisions.</p><p>During the pandemic, when Rainbow Cone and Buona shops as well as seasonal festivals shut down, they scrambled for a way to make money. Buonavolanto’s cousin came up with the idea of an ice cream truck. They painted an old FedEx truck bright pink with white polka dots and brought it to their Buona Beef parking lots. “We had lines down the block and wrapped around the streets,” said Buonavolanto. The addition of more ice cream trucks was inevitable.</p><p>With the anniversary approaching, Sapp is grateful not only to her family but to the city of Chicago and the loyal customers who have embraced Rainbow Cone for 100 years. The uniqueness of the cone itself is a key to the business’ longevity but Sapp also credits her family’s dedication to quality.</p><p>“A lot of people tend to go cheaper, and we protect the quality of the ice cream. My grandpa always said, ‘You have to have a great product and maintain the integrity of it. And you have to make sure it’s in a clean setting and served with a smile.’ It sounds easy but it’s not.”</p><p>She’s also proud of all the memories Rainbow Cone has created.</p><p>“I call it the mini miracle as it’s still around after the Depression and wars and all the other challenges,” Sapp said. “As complicated as people get, it's still a basic ice cream cone and one of the beauties of it is you have to sit back, relax and just enjoy it.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e30000" name="module-e30000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Taste the Rainbow Cone</h3><br>In honor of its 100th anniversary, Rainbow Cone is marking the occasion with events leading up to its centennial birthday on Aug. 9. Here’s how you can celebrate Chicago’s famous five-layer sweet treat.<br><br><b>Immerse yourself in ice cream</b><br><br>Through Aug. 3, Rainbow Cone and the Museum of Ice Cream Chicago are collaborating on a new two-room exhibition featuring storytelling and sensory discovery. Guests can step into a dreamy space highlighting the Rainbow Cone and enjoy samples of the cold confection before exploring an interactive retrospective chronicling the business’ history.<br><br><b>Coming soon to an event near you</b><br><br>Throughout the summer, Rainbow Cone trucks will pop up at community events across the area. Partners include Lookingglass Theatre Company, Pat Mac’s Pack and Lurie Children’s Hospital of Chicago, alongside additional community organizations and neighborhood initiatives to support nonprofit fundraising efforts and youth programming.<br><br>Dates and locations for the Centennial Summer Surprise Tour will be announced throughout the summer at <a class="Link" href="https://rainbowcone.com/" target="_blank" >rainbowcone.com</a>, and on Instagram and Facebook.<br><br><b>South Side team up</b><br><br>Throughout the season, the first 15,000 fans who enter Rate Field for a White Sox home game will receive a special Five-Flavor Game Card that can be redeemed for a free small cone at participating locations if the Sox score in the fourth inning.<br><br><b>Birthday party on Aug. 9</b><br><br>The big birthday bash takes place where it all began at Rainbow Cone’s original neighborhood of Beverly on Aug. 9, where guests ordering the iconic five-flavor cone can spin a prize wheel for the chance to win everything from free treats and merchandise to a Rainbow Cone Truck party valued at $1,000 for you and all of your ice-cream-loving friends.<br><br><i>-Dorothy Hernandez</i></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Rescued belugas have arrived in Chicago. The move is unprecedented — and controversial
entries.summary: <p>In special steel containers marked “live animals, this side up,” the mammoth sea creatures arrived in Chicago in the pre-dawn hours Tuesday.</p><p>It was the first phase of a beluga whale rescue mission Shedd Aquarium staff call “urgent” and “unprecedented.”</p><p>Lori Marino, an animal rights advocate, says it never should have come to this.</p><p>She and others like her envisioned the belugas making their home in a cordoned-off cove along Nova Scotia’s northeastern shore.</p><p>“It’s the best possible solution. Even though it’s still captivity, we are giving them back as much as we possibly can — what was taken from them in the entertainment industry,” said Marino, co-founder and president of the planned $15 million Whale Sanctuary Project in Port Hilford Bay, Nova Scotia.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f90000" name="image-f90000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/de714cf/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+131/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2F12%2Fdf011b4e43fd8c92d972fa7ddd43%2Fbeluga-rescue-821a3554.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/23b2fcd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+131/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2F12%2Fdf011b4e43fd8c92d972fa7ddd43%2Fbeluga-rescue-821a3554.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/114d6dd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+131/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2F12%2Fdf011b4e43fd8c92d972fa7ddd43%2Fbeluga-rescue-821a3554.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Belugas arrive at Shedd Aquarium on Tuesday, July 21, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/114d6dd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+131/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2F12%2Fdf011b4e43fd8c92d972fa7ddd43%2Fbeluga-rescue-821a3554.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/014e36b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+131/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2F12%2Fdf011b4e43fd8c92d972fa7ddd43%2Fbeluga-rescue-821a3554.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/114d6dd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+131/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2F12%2Fdf011b4e43fd8c92d972fa7ddd43%2Fbeluga-rescue-821a3554.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Four belugas, all female, arrived Tuesday morning at Shedd Aquarium.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>©Shedd Aquarium/Heidi Zeiger</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Instead, four of the 30 belugas at the shuttered Marineland aquatic park in Niagara Falls, Ontario, were settling in at Shedd Tuesday. Named Acadia, Lillooet, Osiris and Sierra, the Chicago belugas are all females. Shedd officials said they were chosen to move together “because of their preexisting bonds with one another.” The youngest is 21 years old, while the oldest of the four is 27.</p><p>“While the whales have arrived safely, a transport effort of this magnitude is difficult, and the aquarium cautions that experts expect to learn more about the rescued belugas’ health and current condition in the coming days,” Shedd announced in a news release.</p><p>Some Canadian animal rights advocates have been sounding the alarm for years about animal welfare concerns at Marineland, including cramped tanks and poor water quality. They argue the whales shouldn’t be going from one “concrete tank” to another, and exporting them to Shedd and other aquariums outside the country may even violate Canadian law.</p><p>“The real concern that I and others have is ensuring that Shedd and the other aquariums aren’t going to breed the belugas,” said Camille Labchuk, executive director of Animal Justice, a Toronto-based animal law advocacy group. “If they breed them, that will completely undermine Canada’s national laws, which intended for this generation of whales to be the last suffering in captivity.”</p><p>Johnny Ford, a Shedd spokesman, said "right now, the entire focus of our animal care team is on facilitating a safe rescue."</p><p>But he didn't rule out the Marineland belugas being bred at some point.</p><p>“In the future, if belugas from Marineland were to breed at the aquarium, it would be no different than the way that any other species that is managed by Shedd would breed and that is guided by scientific research, by [Association of Zoos and Aquariums] accreditation standards. … It’s data-informed and it’s always done responsibly.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div The park has drawn protesters for years, accusing Marineland of poor treatment of animals. A total of more than 20 whales and dolphins have died at the park since 2019, according to media reports. Changing cultural attitudes about keeping animals in captivity also contributed to dwindling attendance.</p><p>Labchuk last stepped inside Marineland in 2021.</p><p>“They had dolphins spinning in the air to the [Lou Bega] song, ‘Mambo No. 5.’ That tells you all you need to know,” she said.</p><p>The park closed permanently to the public in 2024. Numerous online drone videos show the belugas languishing in grubby tanks.</p><p>The question then was how best to care for the remaining animals?</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-060000" name="image-060000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c255f6c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F08%2F64%2Fcccd068c455d9e7054af6472e9f8%2Fbeluga-rescue-1482.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ea04882/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F08%2F64%2Fcccd068c455d9e7054af6472e9f8%2Fbeluga-rescue-1482.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2ab3300/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F08%2F64%2Fcccd068c455d9e7054af6472e9f8%2Fbeluga-rescue-1482.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Steel containers containing beluga whales arrived at the Shedd Aquarium before dawn on Tuesday, July 21, 2026. The whales were being transported to the Shedd from the shuttered Marineland park in Niagara Falls, Canada. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2ab3300/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F08%2F64%2Fcccd068c455d9e7054af6472e9f8%2Fbeluga-rescue-1482.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/25e243f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F08%2F64%2Fcccd068c455d9e7054af6472e9f8%2Fbeluga-rescue-1482.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/2ab3300/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F08%2F64%2Fcccd068c455d9e7054af6472e9f8%2Fbeluga-rescue-1482.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The steel containers containing the beluga whales from Marineland arrived in the pre-dawn hours on Tuesday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>©Shedd Aquarium/Heidi Zeiger</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Marino, a neuroscientist and New York University professor, is among a group of animal welfare advocates who, about 11 years ago, began searching for a coastal sanctuary to take up to a dozen captive whales. It would be the first whale sanctuary in North America.</p><p>The group settled on a wooded cove in northeastern Nova Scotia, leasing from the Canadian government an area of coastal water the equivalent of about 100 acres. A wall of netting would prevent the whales from venturing into the open ocean.</p><p>“Having lived in tanks — most of them have been born in tanks — they’re missing all the skills they would need to feed themselves, to form a social group [in open water],” Marino said. “It would be disastrous.”</p><p>Here, harbor seals glide through its slate-blue waters and rock crab scuttle across its sandy bottom. On the shore, black bear and white-tailed deer roam through stands of white spruce and balsam fir.</p><p>The group broke ground on the sanctuary several weeks ago and has raised from private donations and foundations about half of the $15 million they say they need to open.</p><p>Labchuk, a whale sanctuary supporter, said the project would be further along with help from the Canadian federal government.</p><p>“We’ve been telling them for close to a decade that they should be supporting this and that hasn’t materialized,” Labchuk said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Labchuk</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Meanwhile, Marineland applied for permits in September 2025 to have the whales shipped to a theme park in China. Joanne Thompson, Canada’s minister of Fisheries, denied the permits, saying the transfer was not in the best interests of the whales.</p><p>Marineland promptly wrote back to Thompson and, citing Marineland’s “critical financial state,” said: “Our only options at this point are to relocate the whales or face the devastating decision of euthanasia.”</p><p>The Sun-Times tried to reach representatives from Marineland for comment but had not heard back as of late Tuesday afternoon.</p><p>Earlier this year, Marineland and Canada’s Accredited Zoos and Aquariums asked Shedd, among others, to investigate rescuing the belugas, Shedd has said.</p><p>And on Monday, four of the 30 whales were hoisted out of the water in special slings and loaded into containers before being flown out of Canada to Chicago, according to Canadian media reports.</p><p>Four belugas, all female, arrived Tuesday morning.</p><p>“Currently, the animal care teams at  Shedd are working around-the-clock, looking after the rescued whales, providing immediate care and acclimating the animals. For now, caretakers are moving at each individual whale’s pace, and the rescued belugas are not viewable by the public,” Shedd said Tuesday.</p><p>The newcomers join Shedd’s existing group of eight belugas, which can grow up to 18 feet long and weigh about 3,000 pounds. </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Possible violation of Canadian law</b></h3><p>But Marino, Labchuk and other animal welfare advocates say none of the belugas should be shipped out without first having, at the very least, assurances from the receiving aquariums that they won’t breed the animals.</p><p>A 2019 Canadian law, among other things, bans breeding whales in captivity on Canadian soil. The government’s own policy says an application for export permits must show a commitment from the receiving facility that it “will not breed or impregnate the cetacean being exported from Canada.”</p><p>“The government’s own policies say they should not be exported if they are going to be bred, yet the government seems to have [stepped back] from that position,” Labchuk said. “They are not confirming to us that they are putting that condition on the permits.”</p><p>In January, Thompson, the Canadian fishery minister, met with Canadian reporters and was asked about approving the export permits without including a provision that they not be used for breeding in captivity.</p><p>“My confidence in this is that it includes all of the [Marineland] belugas and the dolphins,” Thompson said. “The sites are accredited — the highest standards for animal welfare in the world.”</p><p>Labchuk said her organization hasn’t ruled out legal action. The Canadian law states marine mammals should be exported only when it’s in their “best interests.”</p><p>“It’s a pretty novel test under the law, and that goes for really anywhere around the planet,” Labchuk said. “Usually when we look at animals, what’s important under the law is the interests of the people who own them.”</p><p>Marino, meanwhile, acknowledges the U.S. receiving aquariums, which also include Georgia Aquarium, SeaWorld San Antonio and SeaWorld San Diego, offer a better life than Marineworld.</p><p>“But this is not what they deserve,” she said. “They deserve a very different life in a sanctuary where they can actually have the ability to thrive.”</p>

entries.title: At 250, here's what the U.S. can learn from Lithuania, a younger democracy aided by Chicagoans
entries.summary: <p>VILNIUS, Lithuania — The cafes and bars in Vilnius, Lithuania's capital, bustle with fashionably dressed 20-somethings listening to music, sipping mango matchas and drinking local craft beer — what you'd expect in one of the most vibrant economies in Europe and a place recently pegged as having "the world’s happiest young people."</p><p>Thirty-six years after becoming the first Soviet republic to declare independence and more than two decades after joining the European Union, Lithuania is home to six tech unicorns, startups valued at more than $1 billion. </p><p>It's also a place where as prosperity has risen, voter participation has dropped.</p><p>But over the past 10 months, Lithuania has shown it hasn't lost its pro-democracy roots. Thousands of Lithuanians have taken to the streets, most recently in April, to stand up for democracy and freedom of expression, after a right-wing populist party in the government's ruling coalition tried to control the country's Ministry of Culture and threatened the independence of its public broadcaster Lithuanian Radio and Television.</p><p>Povilas Ušinskis, 18, traveled two and a half hours to march under drizzly skies in Cathedral Square in April. He was marching in support of LRT's editorial independence, during a protest with an estimated 25,000 people.</p><p>"It’s every citizen's right, and in a way, a responsibility," Ušinskis says.</p><p>Protester Milda Valančiauskienė, 53, worries about the rise of authoritarianism around the world.</p><p>"We Lithuanians, we feel when it's dangerous," she says. "We feel it's approaching, even before the real action happens."</p><p>The small country of 2.8 million people — slightly more than Chicago's population — has some lessons for the U.S. about democracy as it celebrates its 250th anniversary.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" data-align-center> <a Sunday</h3><p>Lithuania is filled with people who talk about the "before," the years under Soviet occupation, and the "after," or the period since the early '90s.</p><p>Artūras Pakėnas, 70, who works as a driving instructor in Vilnius, remembers the perilous time around independence — a fight assisted by diaspora Lithuanians in Chicago, who number around 60,000.</p><p>Lithuanians had been organizing for years before they declared their independence on March 11, 1990. The Soviet government responded with an economic blockade, then sent tanks and troops.</p><p>On Lithuania's "Bloody Sunday," Jan. 13, 1991, Soviet soldiers killed 14 Lithuanians who were trying to stop the seizure of the Vilnius TV Tower.</p><p>Other Soviet troops tried to storm the parliament building, but 50,000 citizens became human shields and protected the building.</p><p>One of them was Pakėnas, who was at a friend's birthday party when things started to unravel.</p><p>"From what I saw on TV, this was not going to be good, and I needed to go out," he recalls through a translator, while sipping coffee at a sunny cafe in a Vilnius shopping mall.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>An ongoing fight</h3><p>Organizations that track democracy and authoritarianism worldwide rank Lithuania on the upswing and the U.S. as backsliding.</p><p>The V-Dem Institute at Sweden's University of Gothenburg put Lithuania in the top tier as a "liberal democracy," in a 2026 report ranking countries based on factors such as rule of law, freedom of academic expression, public deliberation and media censorship.</p><p>It downgraded the U.S. to an "electoral democracy" for the first time in 50 years. The report highlighted a "rapid and aggressive concentration of powers in the presidency" during President Donald Trump's second term, along with a lack of legislative constraints. It said "the speed with which American democracy is currently [being] dismantled is unprecedented in modern history."</p><p>The Washington, D.C.,-based nonprofit Freedom House gave Lithuania a higher score, 90 out of 100, on its 2026 Freedom in the World map, compared to 81 for the U.S.</p><p>Meanwhile, the percentage of Americans who see a democratically elected government as "extremely" or "very" important to America's identity dropped from about 80% in 2021 to about 66% this year, according to an AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll. For Americans under 30, the drop is even more striking — only about half share that belief.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c30000" name="module-c30000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h4>7 centuries in 7 sentences: A brief primer on Lithuanian history</h4><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-e95b7b81-7ca9-11f1-a759-29b9b646f68b" start="1"><li>A grand beginning: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania was founded in the early 13th century, and by 1440, the multiethnic state stretching from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea was the superpower of Europe.</li><li>The Polish-Lithuania Commonwealth lasted from 1569 to the late 1700s, when Lithuania diminished in power and was gobbled up by Russia.</li><li>In 1918, Lithuania won its independence, but it was relatively short-lived.</li><li>The secret Molotov-Ribbentrop pact between Germany and the Soviet Union emboldened the Soviet Union to invade and occupy Lithuania in 1940; Lithuanian “enemies of the people” were arrested, and thousands of Lithuanians were sent to Soviet gulags in Siberia.</li><li>In June 1941, Germany broke the pact and invaded Lithuania, and over the next three years, about 195,000 Jewish Lithuanians, or about 95% of Lithuania’s Jewish population, were murdered.</li><li>The Soviets returned in 1944 to push out the Nazis, deporting more than 100,000 Lithuanians to Siberia.</li><li>A reform movement called Sąjūdis began to take hold in the late 1980s, and on March 11, 1990, Lithuania became the first of the Soviet republics to declare independence.</li></ol><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-580000" name="html-embed-module-580000"></a><div id="cpm-gfx--lithdemocracy--sidebar-selector-base"> <!-- This element is here so we can select just the <ol> within this same rich text module rather than either a) being overly specific about IDs that are autogenerated and could change or b) being overly broad and affecting other modules in the same story. --> </div> <style> #cpm-gfx--lithdemocracy--sidebar-selector-base { display: none; He remembers everyone watching the news on TV, until soldiers stormed the national broadcaster's building and pulled the plug.</p><p>"The visuals of January 13 — the anchor on TV, who says [of the soldiers], 'They are walking down the corridor. They're approaching. They're smashing the door,' and then it goes off. That's the first thing you remember," he says.</p><p>Another image seared into his mind was the next morning, walking to the store with his grandmother and seeing sections of the sidewalk shredded by
