class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Karolis Kaupinas, 38, a journalist turned filmmaker and playwright, sits in the lobby of the Lithuanian National Drama Theatre in Vilnius on April 14.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Kaupinas has been busy with projects, including his new play, "Lithuanian Death Notices: The Story of a Performance," inspired by a Facebook page he'd seen of a Chicago funeral home.</p><p>But in September, alarm bells from his childhood went off.</p><p>The populist right-wing party Nemunas Dawn, which had been invited into a governing coalition by the center-left Social Democrats, tried to take over the culture ministry. Then there was a legislative attempt to curtail Lithuanian Radio and Television's editorial independence.</p><p>Kaupinas has helped lead protests for freedom of expression that have expanded across the country. Nemunas Dawn was kicked out of the government in June.</p><p>"I have two small kids now, and they're going to live here after me. And if I want them to have a happy life ... I need to leave it to them as good as I found it," Kaupinas says.</p><p>As for Americans, he hopes they reflect on how fragile freedom can be.</p><p>"Two hundred fifty years of democracy — I’ll make it a bit blunt — makes you lazy," he says. "Americans have been sent to wars, but they haven't seen something like that on their own land for quite some time. I think it's a natural cycle of a society to forget things that shouldn't be taken for granted. That's our danger as well. That's why we are trying to remember that freedom of speech, democracy — that might disappear. It's always easy to destroy things but very hard to create them, to rebuild them."</p><h3>Suburban hotline</h3><p>Watching the recent protests from Chicago's suburbs are George and Viligailė Lendraitis of Palos Heights and Rimas and Audronė Gulbinas of Winfield. The longtime friends helped play a role in bolstering Lithuania's independence 36 years ago.</p><p>Like many Lithuanian Americans in the Chicago area, their family members fled the country and spent decades praying for its independence.</p><p>The language classes, dance troupes and summer camps they joined kept diaspora Lithuanians connected to the culture. That's still the case: Several thousand people attended the Lithuanian Folk Dance Festival of North America in July at the McCormick Center.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div like Lithuania's nascent independence movement might be crushed, the friends created the Lithuanian Hotline to push reports from Lithuania to U.S. government officials, the media and democracy supporters.</p><p>They established a command room at the Lithuanian World Center in Lemont, a 125,000-square-foot facility that hosts more than 50 Lithuanian organizations, including folk dancing groups, a Lithuanian language Montessori preschool and the Lituanica basketball club that helped produce Bulls star Matas Buzelis.</p><p>Illinois Bell hooked up the number they'll never forget: 708-257-6777.</p><p>"We didn’t want any false information going out," George Lendraitis, 77, says. "We were worried. We all have relatives there."</p><p>The hotline transitioned to Lithuanian Mercy Lift, a massive volunteer effort to ship nearly $127 million worth of medicine, medical equipment and other humanitarian supplies to support Lithuania over the next 20 years.</p><p>At a 2010 farewell event in Vilnius' Old Town, doctors, nurses and former President Valdas Adamkus — whose wife volunteered on the hotline when the couple lived in the Chicago suburbs — came out to thank the group.</p><p>"We were happy but exhausted after 20 years," George Lendraitis says. "It was a big part of our life."</p><p>Former Lithuanian President Dalia Grybauskaitė, visiting Chicago for the folk dance festival, called that Chicago support "very important" because it came from a Lithuanian community that also was a bridge to the West. </p><p>"For us, it was a dream about freedom, and this example of the U.S. was helping us to be strong," she says.</p><div class="Enhancement" "They can live in freedom. They can pursue their own goals. They can do what they want without some foreign government or some oppressor saying, 'No, you can't' — stopping people wherever they want to go. So that [American] example of freedom and of democracy flourishing here in Lithuania is really critical."</p><p>Tomas Morkus finished high school this year in Lithuania's second largest city, Kaunas. He spent the 2023-24 school year studying at St. Ignatius College Prep in Chicago on a full scholarship. He'll attend Brown University in the fall.</p><p>Having grown up hearing stories of relatives exiled to Siberia, Morkus says he recognizes that economic prosperity, democracy and defense are intertwined — and that they're worth protecting.</p><p>In high school, he volunteered on numerous projects, including an EU initiative to teach younger kids about the importance of democracy.</p><p>"There are plenty of examples from history where authoritarianism wins against weak democratic institutions or a weak civil society, and then horrible things follow, whether it's Soviet Russia, Hitler's Germany or anywhere else," he says.</p><p>Lithuanians, "still remember the days when they couldn't stand up for themselves and they were shut down for what they say or what they do or what they express," he says. "So I think definitely, the fight is there. The fight is actively going on. I’m proud to be a part of it."</p><p><i>Contributing: Ashlee Rezin</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-fullBleed> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a He spent the 2023-24 school year studying at St. Ignatius College Prep in Chicago and plans to attend Brown University in the fall.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-540000" name="module-540000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h4>When Soviet soldiers stormed a TV station</h4><br>VILNIUS, Lithuania — On Jan. 13, 1991, Soviet troops stormed the building of Lithuania’s public broadcaster and pulled the plug during a live newscast.<br><br>A few minutes earlier, soldiers had begun shooting and driving tanks toward civilians who had gathered to defend the iconic 1,071-foot Vilnius TV Tower in another part of the capital. Fourteen people were killed and hundreds injured.<br><br>Archival video captured the moment, around 2 a.m., when Lithuanian Radio and Television anchor Eglė Bučelytė told viewers another group of soldiers had just breached their offices. <br><br>Soldiers streamed through the hallways.<br><br>“Dear people, this is the very last piece of information: The Lithuanian radio has stopped broadcasting, but television, as you can see, still is,” Bučelytė says.<br><br>But just as quickly, she’s gone; the broadcast shuts off.<br><br>Guoda Litvaitienė was a radio producer at LRT, assigned to work on programs for Lithuanians living abroad.<br><br>Litvaitienė, now 63 and editor-in-chief of LRT Radio, remembers the tense atmosphere that began two days earlier, when Soviet troops seized the National Defense Department building and the Press House, home to most of Lithuania’s newspapers and publishers.<br><br>Litvaitienė’s editor sent her and many other employees home, so she was glued to the same broadcast as everyone else in the country.<br><br>“It was horrible, and nobody knew what would be the ending — will they shoot or what? It was terrible,” she says.<br><br>The soldiers occupied the LRT building for more than seven months, beaming out Soviet propaganda.<br><br>But LRT’s journalists continued working from other locations. Within days, a makeshift TV studio and transmitter were set up at the barricaded parliament building in Vilnius, where legislators inside and citizens outside had managed to repel Soviet soldiers.<br><br>Litvaitienė’s public radio colleagues borrowed studios in Vilnius, offered by a library for blind people, and were able to continue broadcasting.<br><br>“Somehow [the public] knew where we were stationed, and they brought us cakes, some meals, flowers, money,” she says.<br><br>After the troops left, it took months to clean up their mess. Litvaitienė says employees found excrement inside destroyed audio equipment and archival tapes that were wrecked and lying on the floor.<br><br>The equipment was replaced, but the bullet holes in the building were left as a reminder for future generations.<br><br>A new battle over the future of Lithuania’s public broadcaster started late last year, after a far-right populist party installed one of their own at the Ministry of Culture. Parliament members tried to push through legislation that would freeze funding for public broadcasting, making it easier to fire LRT’s director general and compromise the broadcaster’s editorial independence.<br><br>Tens of thousands of people protested, and more than 145,000 people signed a petition in support of LRT’s independence.<br><br>The culture minister resigned after one week and was replaced, and some of the most controversial legislative proposals were withdrawn. class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f00000" name="module-f00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h4>A community still thriving</h4><br>VILNIUS, Lithuania — If there’s one idea Viljamas Žitkauskas would like Americans to know, it’s that the deep roots of the Litvaks — Lithuania’s Jewish community — didn’t disappear in World War II.<br><br>Rather, Jewish culture and creativity lives on in those who stayed after the Holocaust and in those who’ve chosen to return, Žitkauskas tells tourists on his Jewish history tours.<br><br>Lithuania had a thriving population of Litvaks, whose members included Rabbi Elijah ben Solomon Zalman, the famous 18th-century Talmudic scholar and mystic; artist Marc Chagall, born in Belarus to a family with Litvak roots; and the forebears of musicians Bob Dylan and Leonard Cohen.<br><br>Up to 95% of Lithuania’s Jews, about 195,000 people, were murdered by Nazis and their local collaborators when Germany occupied Lithuania from 1941 to 1944. Many historians view the killings as the beginning of the Nazis’ “Final Solution,” the genocide of European Jews during World War II.<br><br>Žitkauskas, who helped found the Vilnius Reform congregation Bnei Maskilim, says many tourists come to Lithuania to hear about the Holocaust but end up learning that Litvak history didn’t end there.<br><br>“For many people, they are coming to see the graveyard, and they’re realizing that it’s not really that. It’s a Jewish community, and there are people living here today, and it’s a big surprise for them,” he says.<br><br>Jewish people arrived in the 1300s, when it was the power center of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania — a sprawling, multiethnic empire that stretched from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea and included Lithuania, Belarus, most of Ukraine and parts of Latvia, Poland, Moldova and Russia.<br><br>Signs of a Jewish presence are everywhere. Žitkauskas likes to point out the famous Vilnius Cathedral, adorned with figures of Moses, Abraham and Noah, Jewish figures from the Old Testament. Vilnius was also once called “the Jerusalem of the North.”<br><br>His family, with roots dating to the 1700s, escaped to Russia during the Holocaust but returned to Lithuania after the German army was driven out by the Soviets in 1944.<br><br>Žitkauskas was 10 years old when Lithuania declared its independence from the Soviet Union.<br><br>“I still remember the Russian tanks,” he says. “I’m still from the generation that really appreciates freedom.”<br><br>Žitkauskas offers tours for groups or individuals. His clients often hail from Israel, U.S., South Africa, Australia and Canada — places where Litvaks built new lives.<br><br>He tailors tours to visitors’ needs. If they’ve got old letters or diaries from ancestors who lived in the Baltic countries or Poland, he can take them to the places where their family members lived.<br><br>Some tourists want to dig into the history of famous Orthodox rabbis. Others want a more secular experience, like learning about Jewish art or comparing Lithuanian potato pancakes to the ones their Ashkenazi grandmother used to make.<br><br>“It’s very dependent on the needs and thoughts of customers — what they’re searching for,” he says.<br><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pulitzer Center</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div>Chicago Sun-Times investigative reporter Stephanie Zimmermann and photo editor Ashlee Rezin traveled to Lithuania for two weeks in April as the Pulitzer Center’s 2026 Richard C. Longworth Media fellows. Their aim was to shed light on a region with strong Chicago ties and an increasingly important role on the world stage.<br><br>A member of the European Union and NATO since 2004, Lithuania is a paradox. Its economic growth is in Europe’s top 25%, and it has six tech unicorns, startups valued at more than $1 billion. Yet the country of 2.8 million people is located at one of Europe’s most vulnerable spots for military defense.<br><br>Zimmermann interviewed more than 50 people for the six-story series, from a former president and a current foreign minister to ordinary Lithuanians living at a time of both promise and peril.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Why I traveled 4,700 miles from Chicago to Lithuania
entries.summary: <p>Why Lithuania?</p><p>That's the first thing my editor asked when I proposed applying for a Pulitzer Center grant for journalists to report international stories. The center's <a class="Link" href="https://pulitzercenter.org/blog/pulitzer-center-awards-2026-longworth-fellowships-2-chicago-journalists" target="_blank" >Richard C. Longworth Media Fellowships</a> help journalists write about global issues impacting Chicago and Midwestern readers.</p><p>Chicago has huge ties to the tiny nation northeast of Poland and across the Baltic Sea from Sweden. About 60,000 Lithuanian Americans live in the Chicago area.</p><p>Upton Sinclair's famous socialist novel "The Jungle" made me forever question eating sausage. Its protagonist, the exploited immigrant Jurgis Rudkus, who chased the American dream in Chicago, was Lithuanian.</p><p>Chicago has other famous Lithuanians: Valdas Adamkus, who became president of Lithuania twice; U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin and Matas Buzelis, the Bulls star who played for Lituanica Athletic Club in Lemont as a kid.</p><p>Lithuania is relevant for other reasons, too.</p><p>Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, many in the U.S. have worried about what would happen if Russian President Vladimir Putin tried attacking a European NATO country. Lithuania, a NATO member since 2004, is a prime target; it's sandwiched between Russia's Kaliningrad and Putin's ally Belarus.</p><p>Meanwhile, Lithuanians are known for sticking their necks out for democracy. Chicagoans helped with that when the country pushed for independence, which we should remember as America celebrates its 250th anniversary.</p><p>But there was another reason I wanted to go.</p><p>My late mother was born in Lithuania. She fled as a child when the Soviet reoccupation began in 1944.</p><p>My cellphone's screensaver is a photo of my mom as a baby, sitting on an unused beehive box (honey is big in Lithuania) with her smiling dad standing next to her.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-330000" class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by Stephanie Zimmermann</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>So, with the blessing of the Chicago Sun-Times, I packed my bags and set off in April with Sun-Times photojournalist and editor Ashlee Rezin.</p><p>This was my third trip to Lithuania. I have cousins there, and I've been learning the language, though almost one-third of Lithuanians speak English.</p><p>I was amazed by the generosity of Lithuanians I met. They spent hours talking to me about democracy, defense, history, economics, Adamkus' legacy and how their small country produces so many big basketball stars.</p><p>Maybe their generosity was because American media too often ignores this nation of just 2.8 million people.</p><p>We met Adamkus, who is turning 100 in November, at his elegant home in the woods on the edge of the capital, Vilnius. The former president had been the regional U.S. Environmental Protection Agency administrator in Chicago. He talked about his favorite Chicago newspapers (I gave him a Sun-Times tote bag) and wanted to know how the Deep Tunnel was faring.</p><p>I also interviewed the foreign minister, economics minister, several parliamentarians, including a signer of the 1990 independence declaration, academics, local officials, business leaders, lawyers, journalists and artists.</p><p>I spoke with ordinary people such as a driving instructor, a civics teacher, flea market sellers and high school and college students. More than 50 people shared their perspectives.</p><p>I learned Lithuanians are in a "dangerous neighborhood," meaning where they sit geographically.</p><p>Even though they prepare for the worst, they're proud to live in a country experiencing economic growth, where young people were deemed the "world’s happiest."</p><p>In addition to Vilnius, our reporting took us to Kaunas, the second largest city and the heart of Lithuanian basketball; Klaipėda on the Baltic Sea; the town of Kybartai, bordering Kaliningrad; a Sunday flea market in Kalvarija, a short drive from the Suwalki Gap; Trakai, home of Lithuania's most picturesque castle; and the town of Kazlų Rūda, deep in the pine forests.</p><p>One Sunday morning, we were driving on the back roads of southwest Lithuania with our translator, Karolis Vyšniauskas.</p><p>Vyšniauskas was planning to turn left, heading for Kalvarija, when the road got rough, so we went straight.</p><p>About 100 yards later, I yelled, "Stop!"</p><p>A road sign read "Pajevonys," a name that seemed vaguely familiar. I flipped through my grandparents' memoirs, which I'd packed with my reporting notes.</p><p>My hunch was right. They lived in Pajevonys when my mom was a baby. My grandparents were teachers, and they frequently moved to different towns for jobs.</p><p>Within a few years, they would flee Lithuania. Theirs is a story shared by many in the diaspora: They were "displaced persons" in camps in Germany at the end of World War II. My mom spent her childhood in Germany, then won a college scholarship to study in America and later became a naturalized American citizen.</p><p>Vyšniauskas pulled over, and I hopped out of the car to touch the sign.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-340000" name="image-340000"></a> entries.title: Food brings this family together, but one particular recipe reminds them of home
entries.summary: <p>Food has been at the center of Teddy and Alexis Vejar’s lives since they were kids.</p><p>They remember walking around their neighborhood in Morelia, Michoacán, where people would open up their driveways or garages and serve dinner out of their homes.</p><p>When they moved to Chicago in the 1990s, their dad — who they call “the original Mexican foodie” — still searched far and wide for the best food he could find.</p><p>“We would literally drive from Chicago all the way to Oaxaca, and my dad would say, ‘We’re going to try cabrito (suckling goat),’” Alexis Vejar said. “We would take detours for specific dishes. We would go all the way to Veracruz just to try the pescado a la Veracruzana.”</p><p>Today, the brothers own Jarabe. The restaurant opened in 2015 and prides itself on authentic Mexican cuisine. You won’t find any “fancy tacos” at the Little Italy spot.</p><p>“We could do fancy tacos,” Alexis Vejar said. “But what’s ridiculously good? What my grandma used to do — harvesting the corn, milking the cow, making the cheese, making sour cream. That's more hard work than a Michelin-star restaurant is prepared to do.”</p><p>The brothers have spent 15 years building a menu they can be proud of, and every recipe traces back to what they learned from their parents and grandparents.</p><p>When they began developing their recipes, they focused on making things from scratch, like tortillas and marinades, even when it was more difficult.</p><p>Of all the dishes they grew up eating, one remains their favorite all these years later: cochinita pibil. They serve it at their restaurant.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" data-align-center> <a class="AnchorLink" memories living in Chicago’s Ukrainian Village, when their dad began making homemade cochinita pibil for them and their extended family. Even today, the family gets together to eat the dish.</p><p>Cochinita pibil is a Yucatán-style pulled pork dish. The pork is marinated in achiote paste and served with tortillas and pickled red onions. It’s considered one of Yucatán’s traditional dishes, and it’s a favorite celebration meal for the Vejar family.</p><p>The dish reminds them of when their dad would cook it for them when they were kids.</p><p>“My dad's really into analyzing dishes and seeing how you can improve them, so that was part of the fun,” Alexis Vejar said. “It's something that Teddy and I ate a lot in Morelia because there was one puestito that sold cochinita pibil. We just rolled up to the tiny place that sold these tiny little tacos with the little red onions on top. We were obsessed with them. It just reminded us so much of home.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2026/07/22/cochinita-pibil-recipe" >Bring this cochinita pibil recipe to your next family dinner</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Looking back to their time in Mexico, Alexis and Teddy reflected on how simple the recipes seemed in theory, though they now realize the immense time and process everything entailed. Corn was grown and harvested, then went through the nixtamalization process — a tradition they maintain at their restaurant today to craft their own homemade tortillas.</p><p>“Every time we visited my grandma, she was waking up and making homemade bread with natural yeast that she was cultivating in a wood-burning oven,” Alexis Vejar said. “If we had sour cream or cheese, she milked the cow to make it. If we had meat, it was meat that they raised, that they butchered, that they cured. The menus were all limited by what was available on the farm.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/OazrsIWZC3Q?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Tastes from Home: Tortillas, togetherness and time well spent."></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Even after years in business, Alexis and Teddy say they're still learning and growing.</p><p>Running a restaurant is nonstop, but they remain committed to honoring the family traditions that started long before Jarabe opened.</p><p>“We haven't slowed down. entries.title: Benet's Ed Stasys getting long-overdue attention
entries.summary: <p>Benet’s Ed Stasys has never garnered as much attention or recognition as he deserved.</p><p>In helping Benet compile a whopping 69 wins over the past two seasons, including a state championship in 2025 and a state runner-up finish in 2026, the stats Stasys put up have never been sufficient enough to merit the enormous attention others have received in the sport.</p><p>When your greatest accomplishments are in the game’s subtleties in seeking victories for a team, it takes a close observer to really notice. Watching Stasys, you could never place a statistical value on all that he has meant to a team’s winning.</p><p>“Ed was mature enough to understand that he was an important part of the team while understanding his role,” Benet coach Gene Heidkamp said. “He understood the sacrifice on his part was for the betterment of team success.”</p><p>But the impact was still present, even if the gaudy stats weren’t. Opposing coaches saw the influence he made in a game and were forced to game plan for him.</p><p>There is the elite defense, including the ability to guard multiple positions all over the floor while contesting shots at the rim. He makes hard cuts and sets solid screens. And at 6-8 he beats others to the ball and opponents down the floor as a rim-running big man.</p><p>“He gets out in front on the break and collapses a defense in transition, drawing the attention of a defense and creating space for our shooters,” Heidkamp pointed out. “That’s just one example of his impact and how he factors into a game without even sometimes touching the ball.”</p><p>But the toughness, hustle, physicality and spirit he plays with are the traits that really resonate. He channels his competitiveness into the greater good of the team, setting the tone and effort of the team.</p><p>Starting his 34th season as a high school basketball coach, Heidkamp says Stasys showcases one of the best motors he’s ever been around.</p><p>“He never takes a possession off in a game or in a practice,” Heidkamp said.</p><p>Stasys, who averaged a rock solid 12 points and over six rebounds a game last season, has never worried about compiling headlines or accolades for himself.</p><p>“My only focus is to keep on working hard and to keep getting better,” Stasys said of the lack of early individual recognition. “I thought eventually everything would fall into place as they should.”</p><p>Stasys quickly realized every component of basketball mattered, thanks to the mindset and mentality ingrained by Heidkamp and his father, Tomas.</p><p>“Honestly, a lot of it comes from coach Heidkamp and the Benet program,” Stasys said. “Being part of the Benet program is like an honor, especially playing for coach Heidkamp. I was pretty much just a role player at the start, but coach Heidkamp has always believed in me and has told me to do the little things.”</p><p>Then there was a dad who put it simply and kept it real with his son.</p><p>“My dad always tells me to just do whatever it takes to win and contribute in any way possible,” Stasys said. “And now I would rather win than have a performance all about me. I think winning is more important, and that’s just what I value.”</p><p>The lack of notoriety and attention? Those days are over. Stasys’ combined play this spring and summer with Benet and with the Illinois Wolves on the club basketball circuit has created a stir.</p><p>“He was an important piece of the puzzle as a sophomore, and he really emerged in his own right last season as a junior,” Heidkamp said. “This year he’s ready to be more of a focal point.”</p><p>He’s made a push to the top of the revamped Class of 2027 player rankings in Illinois while generating a ton of recruiting interest.</p><p>Blessed with great academics, Stasys is a must-get for Ivy League powers Yale and Harvard, where he says he plans to visit in September. Mid-majors are in full pursuit, high-majors are taking notice with Illinois coach Brad Underwood offering last week.</p><p>“I’ve had dreams of playing Division I basketball, and now with the offers and where recruiting is going, it’s great, everything is falling into place now,” Stasys said. “I have been working my whole life for this. I had hopes that it would play out like this. But I have to keep it going.”</p><p>Stasys is the next in line at Benet to keep the powerhouse basketball program going.</p><p>During Benet’s most recent success, the Redwings have used balance while leaning heavily on the likes of Colin Stack (North Dakota State), Jayden Wright (Eastern Illinois), Blake Fagbemi (Illinois) and Daniel Pauliukonis (Southern Illinois), who have all graduated and moved on to Division I basketball over the past two years. Now Stasys, who is a more coveted prospect than all of them, understands it's his time to lead a team that is expected to again be one of the state’s best.</p><p>“I haven’t always had the biggest role, but I’ve been around winning players and I have seen what it takes to win and what you have to do to contribute to winning,” Stasys said. “I’ve always been a player that will do what you need me to do. But as I get older, my role and confidence keeps building and growing. I’m ready for what’s ahead.”</p>

entries.title: Mexican Sinaloa cartel drug lord Ismael ‘El Mayo’ Zambada, sentenced to life in prison, denounces violence
entries.summary: <p>Mexican drug kingpin Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada was sentenced in a U.S. court on Monday to life in prison and took the occasion to call for an end to the brand of brutal violence that he used to build the Sinaloa cartel into what prosecutors said was the world’s largest drug-trafficking organization.</p><p>“No one wins in a war like this,” Zambada, 76, said in federal court in Brooklyn through a Spanish-language translator.</p><p>With cartel co-founder <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/el-chapo" target="_blank" ><u>Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzmán Loera</u></a> — who was convicted in 2019 and is serving a life sentence at the federal Supermax prison in Florence, Colorado — Zambada flooded Chicago, a key hub in the Sinaloa cartel's network, and cities across the United States with tons of cocaine, fentanyl, methamphetamine and other drugs. Chicago-based investigations helped lead to the downfall of both men.</p><p>Zambada “spent nearly four decades poisoning American communities to make billions of dollars in profit and ordering the murders of anyone who stood in his way,” Brooklyn U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said. “Today, that chapter closes for good.”</p><p>Violence was Zambada’s “tool for more than three decades when it benefited him,” according to Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Amir, who said Zambada ordered torture and plotted killings — including that of his own nephew.</p><p>During Zamada's reign, more than 1 million Americans died of overdoses — many from drugs from Mexico or the Sinaloa cartel, Amir said.</p><p>Zambada's punishment was set in stone when he pleaded guilty last year to drug-trafficking charges that carry a mandatory life sentence. He also faces $15 billion in financial penalties related to proceeds from the cartel’s crimes, but prosecutors said they haven’t been able to identify or recover any assets.</p><p>After causing untold violence and crime, Zambada said in court that he's sorry “for the harm I caused and for the example I set." And he urged young people to “choose a different path.”</p><p>“If there’s one thing I can say that has value today, it’s this: The violence must end,” the cartel co-founder said. “In Mexico and elsewhere affected by this type of crime, too many lives are lost, too many families are destroyed, and too many young people are trapped in a cycle that leads only to prison or death.”</p><p>Zambada's sentencing by U.S. District Judge Brian M. Cogan was the culmination of a yearslong fight by the U.S. government to bring the long-elusive drug lord to justice. He was arrested in 2024 after he said he was kidnapped in Mexico and flown to Texas.</p><p>Cogan, acting on a request by Zambada's lawyer, said he will recommend that he serve his sentence at a federal prison hospital where he can be treated for what his lawyer described as a “complex of age-related health issues.”</p><p>The judge ordered Zambada’s medical records sealed from public view but said he suffers from a number of “progressive illnesses” and that his mental state is “drifting toward cognitively impaired."</p><p>Judges often make recommendations about where inmates should serve time, but it’s up to the federal Bureau of Prisons to decide.</p><p>Zambada’s lawyer Frank Perez said in court that the drug lord wasn’t cooperating with prosecutors. But, in arguing to have him sent to a prison hospital, Perez contrasted Zambada’s guilty plea to Guzmán’s decision to go to trial — an 11-week saga that involved closing down the Brooklyn Bridge so he could be shuttled to and from court and jail.</p><h3>Sinaloa cartel’s dealmaker</h3><p>Zambada was seen as the Sinaloa cartel’s strategist and dealmaker and was more involved in its day-to-day operations than El Chapo.</p><p>Zambada was arrested in July 2024 after, according to Perez, he was beaten, tied up, abducted and driven to a private plane by one of Guzmán’s sons, Joaquín Guzmán López. Their arrests touched off deadly fighting in Sinaloa that pitted Zambada loyalists against backers of Guzmán’s sons, dubbed the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/el-chapo/2024/05/31/elchapo-chapo-sinaloa-cartel-bounty-nestor-isidro-perez-salas-chapitos-dea" ><i>Chapitos</i></a>, or “little Chapos.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/el-chapo/2025/08/25/chapo-elchapo-sinaloa-cartel-ismael-zambada-elmayo-mayo-guilty-plea-mexican-drug-lord-joaquin-guzman-loera" target="_blank" >Zambada pleaded guilty in August 2025</a> to charges of engaging in a continuing criminal enterprise and racketeering conspiracy, acknowledging culpability for 85 underlying crimes, after prosecutors agreed not to seek the death penalty.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-390000" know would’ve been very difficult.”</p><p>Zambada, wearing a tan jail suit over an orange T-shirt, walked gingerly as deputy federal marshals escorted him to and from the courtroom, which was packed with drug enforcement agents and prosecution staff members. The top federal prosecutors in Brooklyn, Miami and western Texas watched from the gallery.</p><p>In pleading guilty, Zambada said that, from 1980 until last year, he and his cartel were responsible for transporting at least 3.3 million pounds of cocaine, “most of which went to the United States.”</p><p>Zambada, the father of 16 children ranging in age from 6 to 55, said he first got into the drug trade as a marijuana grower in 1969 after leaving school with a sixth-grade education.</p><p>He acknowledged the scope of the Sinaloa operation, including underlings who built relationships with Colombian cocaine producers, oversaw importing cocaine to Mexico by boat and plane and smuggling the drug across the U.S.-Mexico border. He said the cartel took in hundreds of millions of dollars a year and admitted that people working for him paid hefty bribes to Mexican officials “so they could operate freely.”</p><p>Months before Zambada's arrest, prosecutors said, he ordered the killing of his nephew Eliseo Imperial Castro, known as “Cheyo Antrax,” after finding out that Castro was claiming to be collecting debts for Zambada and pocketing the money without Zambada’s permission.</p><p>In 2023, at least three people were killed in retaliatory violence that Zambada directed after a large cache of fentanyl pills, methamphetamine and cocaine was stolen from the cartel, according to prosecutors.</p><p>“I grew up in an environment where violence and crime seemed normal, but now I know that’s no excuse,” Zambada said in court. “There comes a time when every person must take responsibility for their decisions. I didn’t, and many people paid the price.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li entries.title: Results of Nolan Wells autopsy to be released at NAACP Chicago conference
entries.summary: <p>An attorney for the family of Nolan Xavier Wells says he will release the results of an independent autopsy into the 18-year-old's death on Wednesday morning.</p><p>The preliminary findings are set to be made public during a news conference held at the annual NAACP National Convention in Chicago, according to the civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who is representing the family. Wells' parents are expected to attend.</p><p>Crump has vowed to conduct his own investigation into the circumstances of the teenager's disappearance, which followed a July 4 boat trip with friends to an island off the coast of Mississippi. Wells did not return to the mainland with his friends. His body was found floating off the island's coast two days later.</p><p>The Mississippi State Medical Examiner's Office conducted its own autopsy but has yet to release the results.</p><p>The second autopsy was arranged by the family and Crump, and paid for by former NFL player Colin Kaepernick. Crump said it would determine if Wells "had any physical injuries to his body beyond drowning."</p><p>The still-unknown circumstances around Wells' death have touched off rampant online speculation and prompted calls from Black leaders for transparency from local authorities. Wells, who was Black, had traveled to the island with a group of high school friends, all of whom are white.</p><p>A reward of $125,000 — jointly funded by the Rev. Al Sharpton, actor and producer Tyler Perry and former NFL player Terrell Owens — is now being offered in exchange for information leading to an arrest and conviction in connection with the death.</p><p>The autopsy announcement comes two days after Wells was laid to rest in his hometown of Ocean Springs, Mississippi.</p><p>In his eulogy, Sharpton lamented the "inconsistencies and unanswered questions" that had placed a dark cloud over the grieving family.</p><p>He questioned why Wells' friends had left him behind, taken his phone and keys and failed to report him missing to police. And he suggested local investigators had spoken prematurely in statements to the press indicating that no crime was suspected.</p><p>"The reason that a lot of people across the nation are looking at this Nolan situation is because we're looking at the history in Mississippi," Sharpton added. "We can't have someone in law enforcement saying there was no foul play before there was an investigation."</p><p>Jackson County Sheriff John Ledbetter said initial interviews suggested Wells chose to stay on the island and that his friends believed he would get a ride with someone else. He has said the friends were cooperating with the investigation, which remains ongoing.</p><p>"We are trying to be respectful and collaborative as much as we can," Crump said. "But it's always troublesome to all of us when these investigations just take forever."<br></p>

entries.title: 2 state troopers injured in crash after driver runs stop sign in Cicero
entries.summary: <p>Two state troopers were injured in a crash after a driver ran a stop sign early Wednesday in west suburban Cicero. </p><p>The state troopers were driving south on Cicero Avenue just after midnight when a driver going east on 14th Street ran a stop sign and t-boned the troopers, Illinois state police said. </p><p>Both troopers and the driver of the other vehicle were taken to area hospitals with unspecified injuries, officials said. </p><p>No further information was immediately available. </p>

entries.title: A root canal AND rotator cuff surgery? Lucky me.
entries.summary: <p>My dentist's office called after a routine cleaning and X-ray. Could I, they wondered, come back? Tomorrow. I got the sense that if I said, "I can rush over right now," they'd reply. "Good, hurry." It was a matter of tone.</p><p>The news was bad. An enormous cavity, growing hidden beside my upper right wisdom tooth. Maybe even invading the jaw bone. Requiring a root canal and crown. I'd probably lose the wisdom tooth too.</p><p>"I like how you're so grim," I told the dentist, after he explained the situation. "It shows you care."</p><p>Off to the endodontist for the root canal. Two hours in the chair. Honestly, it didn't hurt — well, my left arm did, quite a lot, fallout from my ripped-up left shoulder. Holding still for so long. I'd occasionally extend my arm, taking care not to upset a tray of tools. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2f0000" name="module-2f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>Then there was the enforced silence. Although, being me, I still tried to speak, with a dental dam plus dental instruments in my mouth. I wanted to tell the endodontist how important Chicago is to the history of fluoridation. The initial experiments were held in Evanston in 1946, with Oak Park as the control. Being an endodontist, he'd be interested. </p><p>Shutting up is an art form I struggle to master.</p><p>But that isn't the most embarrassing part.</p><p>The root canal was the first act. My next step was back to the dentist, who created a crown to go over the afflicted tooth, shaved down to a stump.</p><p>More than three hours in that chair, including the wait while the crown was sculpted by a high-tech medical printer. When I could speak again, this is what I said:</p><p>"You know what I was thinking for the past two hours? And this will sound like I'm blowing smoke... but I was thinking about how lucky I am to have access to high quality medical care like this."</p><p>I actually said that. And I meant it. Some 100 million Americans don't routinely see a dentist, usually because of the cost. Half the world's population suffers from untreated oral diseases, according to the World Health Organization.</p><p>A reminder. You know what's much worse than having a root canal? Needing one and not getting it.</p><p>Honestly, the root canal/crown was plenty to hone my medical gratitude. But life has a way of laying it on. A couple weeks later, I went to get an MRI on the shoulder that has hurt me since I tripped and fell on a train platform in Portugal. I was hoping the doctor would say it was merely strained, perhaps prescribe the shoulder be massaged with warm healing oils while listening to whale song.</p><p>Torn rotator cuff. Which I could ignore, going to physical therapy, building up the muscles around the detached, nearly useless muscle.</p><p>Or I could have it repaired by arthroscopic surgery. Cut a few holes in my arm, poke in a camera, set some anchors in the bone, sew the muscle back in place, out in an hour. Not even a night's stay in the hospital.</p><p>However. And this is a big honking however. I have to wear my left arm in a sling, 24 hours a day. For six weeks. Lift a coffee cup, scratch my ear, and I could rip out all the surgeon's careful handiwork. The surgeon suggested I do a few months of physical therapy and see where we stood.</p><p>I surprised myself by saying, "Nah, why wait? Let's do the surgery now."</p><p>Why? First, if I'm going to go through months of rehab, why not train a good-as-new rebuilt shoulder instead of the fraying old bum one?</p><p>Here my mother helped, quite the feat, since she's been dead for over a year. But she had a foot that was twisting, and also needed complex orthopedic surgery. She refused, for all the reasons I was tempted to say no — painful, long recovery, outcome uncertain, can blunder forward with it as it is. Eventually she could barely walk, hobbling around the Whole Foods, depending on shopping carts as walkers and the kindness of strangers. Lack of mobility eventually helped kill her.</p><p>My takeaway is: don't neglect problems. Fix them. "God grant me the courage... to change the things I can." Not necessarily for now. But for 10 years from now, when I might be glad that all the muscles in my shoulder work together as a team.</p><p>Which is a long way of saying, this is my last column for at least three weeks. Maybe more. I'm sorry to leave you in the lurch, though my colleagues will keep you informed and entertained. And rest assured, as much as you'll miss me, I'll miss you more, and get back as soon as I can.</p>

entries.title: Man charged with shooting SWAT officer and woman during hostage situation in Albany Park
entries.summary: <p>A man was charged with shooting a SWAT officer and a woman during a standoff Monday in Albany Park on the Northwest Side. </p><p>Daniel Aguirre, 42, faced several felony charges including attempted murder, aggravated discharge of a firearm, aggravated battery, aggravated unlawful restraint, aggravated assault of a peace officer and aggravated discharge of a firearm in an occupied building, Chicago police said</p><p>He was arrested hours after the incident began Monday morning in the 4600 block of North Springfield Avenue, officials said. </p><p>Police responded around 11 a.m. to a call of a female shot in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/20/shooting-in-albany-park-prompts-multi-ambulance-response" target="_blank" >4600 block of North Springfield Avenue</a>, interim Chicago police Supt. Fred Waller told reporters Monday afternoon. An internal police report indicated she had been shot in the face. </p><p>When SWAT officers tried to enter the home, the suspect fired through a door and struck one of the officers in the lower abdomen, according to Waller.</p><p>Aguirre was scheduled to appear in court Wednesday. </p>

entries.title: Boy, 15, found fatally shot in Austin
entries.summary: <p>A 15-year-old boy was found fatally shot early Wednesday in Austin on the West Side. </p><p>Just after 1 a.m., officers and paramedics responded to a call of a person shot in the 4600 block of West Jackson Boulevard and the boy was found shot in the head, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Stroger Hospital where he was pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>Area 4 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Prosecutors reject charges in deadly Lincoln Park shooting that prompted bar’s closure
entries.summary: <p>Prosecutors rejected charges against a person of interest taken into custody after a fatal shooting this weekend near a Lincoln Park bar that has since been closed by the city.</p><p>A spokesperson for Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke said “the evidence doesn’t support criminal charges” in the shooting early Sunday near The Dime, 2263 N. Lincoln Ave. The Dime was later shuttered Tuesday by acting police Supt. Fred Waller.</p><p>Malik McCorkle, 30, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/20/man-shot-and-killed-during-fight-in-lincoln-park-1-in-custody" target="_blank" >shot multiple times</a> and killed outside of a nearby bar called King of Cups, 2238 N. Lincoln Ave. But witnesses said the shooting happened after fights broke out inside of The Dime. An altercation eventually <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/21/shooting-lincoln-park-the-dime-timmy-knudsen-fred-waller" target="_blank" >spilled onto the sidewalk and turned deadly</a>, according to city officials and nearby business owners.</p><p>Local Ald. Timmy Knudsen (43rd) said surveillance video from businesses showed people openly carrying weapons on the block before the shooting happened. He said neighboring establishments turned over footage to detectives.</p><p>“This incident underscores the aggressive work we need to continue to do as a city and state to get guns off of the streets and to prosecute offenders,” Knudsen said in a statement this week.</p><p>His office didn’t respond to an inquiry about charges being rejected in Sunday’s shooting.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/20/man-shot-and-killed-during-fight-in-lincoln-park-1-in-custody" target="_blank" >Man shot to death during bar fight in Lincoln Park</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/21/shooting-lincoln-park-the-dime-timmy-knudsen-fred-waller" target="_blank" >Lincoln Park bar The Dime shut down after deadly weekend shooting</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

target="_blank" >U.S. can learn from Lithuania, a younger democracy aided by Chicagoans</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wutyddk-l-k/" target="_blank" >Stephanie Zimmermann</a></h5><p><b>New series</b>: In April, Sun-Times reporter <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wutyddk-l-u/" target="_blank" >Stephanie Zimmermann</a> and photo desk editor <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wutyddk-l-o/" target="_blank" >Ashlee Rezin</a> traveled to Lithuania on assignment, meeting dignitaries and everyday citizens, traversing its back roads and city streets, and diving into the country's rich history to see how issues there impact Chicago and Midwestern readers. The result: A multipart series launching today.</p><p><b>Why Lithuania?</b>: Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, many in the U.S. have worried what would happen if Russian President Vladimir Putin tried attacking a European NATO country. Lithuania, a NATO member since 2004, is a prime target. The small country of 2.8 million people — slightly more than Chicago’s population — recently celebrated the 36th anniversary of its independence. Lithuanians are known for sticking their necks out for democracy. Chicagoans helped with that when the country pushed for independence.</p><p><b>Baltic connection</b>: Chicago has huge ties to the tiny nation northeast of Poland and across the Baltic Sea from Sweden. Among the city's famous Lithuanians: Valdas Adamkus, who became president of the country twice; U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin; and Matas Buzelis, the Bulls star who played for Lituanica Athletic Club in Lemont. Upton Sinclair's "The Jungle" centers an exploited Lithuanian immigrant. Today, about 60,000 Lithuanian Americans live in the Chicago area.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Pulaski Road is slated to close this weekend.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Owen Ziliak/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wutyddk-l-c/" target="_blank" >Save A Lot stores set to close Saturday after years of turmoil</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wutyddk-l-q/" target="_blank" >Mariah Rush</a></h5><p><b>Stores close</b>: After opening seven Save A Lot discount stores on the South and West sides with a promise to address food deserts, embattled operator Yellow Banana is set to shutter all stores this weekend, leaving some predominantly Black and Brown neighborhoods without a grocery.</p><p><b>Taxpayer funds</b>: Ohio-based Yellow Banana has a redevelopment agreement with the city of Chicago, through which it received more than $13 million in taxpayer financing to renovate and reopen Save A Lot locations. Save A Lot says it's cutting ties with Yellow Banana, and without a corporate sponsor, Yellow Banana is set to close all of its stores.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The news comes years after Yellow Banana operators promised Chicagoans on the South and West sides that they would provide quality food. Citations and penalties for expired foods, upcharging of customers, and overgrown weeds continued throughout the entirety of Yellow Banana’s ownership. But Chicagoans, especially those on the South Side, know that the Original Rainbow Cone shop and its photogenic namesake are local institutions.</p><p>Launched in August 1926 in a small shack at 92nd Street and Western Avenue, Rainbow Cone turns 100 this year with a slew of events to mark the occasion.</p><p>Back when Joe and Katherine Sapp started the business, Beverly was nothing like it is today. The couple saw potential in the area that was dominated by dirt roads and dotted with apple orchards and summer cottages.</p><p>A car mechanic by trade, Joe was inspired to open Rainbow Cone for a simple reason. "He always loved ice cream and was fascinated by it," said Lynn Sapp, the third-generation owner of Rainbow Cone.</p><p>"I call it the mini miracle as it’s still around after the Depression and wars and all the other challenges," Sapp said. "As complicated as people get, it’s still a basic ice cream cone and one of the beauties of it is you have to sit back, relax and just enjoy it."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wutyddk-l-iu/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>What longtime Chicago institution should more people know about?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Email your answer to us</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: Why I traveled 4,700 miles from Chicago to Lithuania
entries.summary: <p>Why Lithuania?</p><p>That's the first thing my editor asked when I proposed applying for a Pulitzer Center grant for journalists to report international stories. The center's <a class="Link" href="https://pulitzercenter.org/blog/pulitzer-center-awards-2026-longworth-fellowships-2-chicago-journalists" target="_blank" >Richard C. Longworth Media Fellowships</a> help journalists write about global issues impacting Chicago and Midwestern readers.</p><p>Chicago has huge ties to the tiny nation northeast of Poland and across the Baltic Sea from Sweden. About 60,000 Lithuanian Americans live in the Chicago area.</p><p>Upton Sinclair's famous socialist novel "The Jungle" made me forever question eating sausage. Its protagonist, the exploited immigrant Jurgis Rudkus, who chased the American dream in Chicago, was Lithuanian.</p><p>Chicago has other famous Lithuanians: Valdas Adamkus, who became president of Lithuania twice; U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin and Matas Buzelis, the Bulls star who played for Lituanica Athletic Club in Lemont as a kid.</p><p>Lithuania is relevant for other reasons, too.</p><p>Since Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, many in the U.S. have worried about what would happen if Russian President Vladimir Putin tried attacking a European NATO country. Lithuania, a NATO member since 2004, is a prime target; it's sandwiched between Russia's Kaliningrad and Putin's ally Belarus.</p><p>Meanwhile, Lithuanians are known for sticking their necks out for democracy. Chicagoans helped with that when the country pushed for independence, which we should remember as America celebrates its 250th anniversary.</p><p>But there was another reason I wanted to go.</p><p>My late mother was born in Lithuania. She fled as a child when the Soviet reoccupation began in 1944.</p><p>My cellphone's screensaver is a photo of my mom as a baby, sitting on an unused beehive box (honey is big in Lithuania) with her smiling dad standing next to her.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-330000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Chicago Sun-Times reporter Stephanie Zimmermann’s mother as a toddler in Lithuania.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by Stephanie Zimmermann</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>So, with the blessing of the Chicago Sun-Times, I packed my bags and set off in April with Sun-Times photojournalist and editor Ashlee Rezin.</p><p>This was my third trip to Lithuania. I have cousins there, and I've been learning the language, though almost one-third of Lithuanians speak English.</p><p>I was amazed by the generosity of Lithuanians I met. They spent hours talking to me about democracy, defense, history, economics, Adamkus' legacy and how their small country produces so many big basketball stars.</p><p>Maybe their generosity was because American media too often ignores this nation of just 2.8 million people.</p><p>We met Adamkus, who is turning 100 in November, at his elegant home in the woods on the edge of the capital, Vilnius. The former president had been the regional U.S. Environmental Protection Agency administrator in Chicago. He talked about his favorite Chicago newspapers (I gave him a Sun-Times tote bag) and wanted to know how the Deep Tunnel was faring.</p><p>I also interviewed the foreign minister, economics minister, several parliamentarians, including a signer of the 1990 independence declaration, academics, local officials, business leaders, lawyers, journalists and artists.</p><p>I spoke with ordinary people such as a driving instructor, a civics teacher, flea market sellers and high school and college students. More than 50 people shared their perspectives.</p><p>I learned Lithuanians are in a "dangerous neighborhood," meaning where they sit geographically.</p><p>Even though they prepare for the worst, they're proud to live in a country experiencing economic growth, where young people were deemed the "world’s happiest."</p><p>In addition to Vilnius, our reporting took us to Kaunas, the second largest city and the heart of Lithuanian basketball; Klaipėda on the Baltic Sea; the town of Kybartai, bordering Kaliningrad; a Sunday flea market in Kalvarija, a short drive from the Suwalki Gap; Trakai, home of Lithuania's most picturesque castle; and the town of Kazlų Rūda, deep in the pine forests.</p><p>One Sunday morning, we were driving on the back roads of southwest Lithuania with our translator, Karolis Vyšniauskas.</p><p>Vyšniauskas was planning to turn left, heading for Kalvarija, when the road got rough, so we went straight.</p><p>About 100 yards later, I yelled, "Stop!"</p><p>A road sign read "Pajevonys," a name that seemed vaguely familiar. I flipped through my grandparents' memoirs, which I'd packed with my reporting notes.</p><p>My hunch was right. They lived in Pajevonys when my mom was a baby. My grandparents were teachers, and they frequently moved to different towns for jobs.</p><p>Within a few years, they would flee Lithuania. Theirs is a story shared by many in the diaspora: They were "displaced persons" in camps in Germany at the end of World War II. My mom spent her childhood in Germany, then won a college scholarship to study in America and later became a naturalized American citizen.</p><p>Vyšniauskas pulled over, and I hopped out of the car to touch the sign.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-340000" name="image-340000"></a> entries.title: Mexico seeks accountability in Chicago-area ICE death and 16 others. Can it force the U.S. to act?
entries.summary: <p>Mexico has begun <a class="Link" href="https://www.gob.mx/presidencia/prensa/vamos-a-hacer-todo-lo-que-este-en-nuestras-manos-presidenta-sre-inicia-acciones-por-muerte-de-mexicanos-en-custodia-y-operativos-de-ice" target="_blank" ><u>taking legal action</u></a> to seek accountability for the deaths of 17 Mexican nationals who have died during U.S.Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations — 14 died in ICE custody, and three were killed during other “arrest operations.” This includes Silverio Villegas González, who was shot and killed by an ICE agent during a traffic stop in Franklin Park nearly a year ago.</p><p>Villegas González had lived in the United States since 2007. He was the father of two young children.</p><p>At the time, the federal Department of Homeland Security said Villegas González had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/09/16/ice-body-cameras-deadly-shooting-silverio-villegas-gonzalez-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>fled a traffic stop and dragged</u></a> an ICE agent “a significant distance with his car,” seriously injuring the agent. But Franklin Park police body-camera video footage obtained by the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/09/22/ice-officer-injuries-nothing-major-deadly-franklin-park-shooting-mexican-immigrant-chicago-video?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=092325%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=092325%20Morning%20Edition+CID_7ddfe7afa69b632582015a9194a33f32&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=ICE%20officer%20said%20his%20injuries%20were%20nothing%20major%20after%20deadly%20shooting%20near%20Chicago%20video%20shows&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Sun-Times cast doubt on DHS’s description of what happened, </u></a>catching the ICE agent saying his injuries were "nothing major," a "knee injury" and "some lacerations" to his hands.</p><p>Mexico’s announcement came days after an ICE agent fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo during a traffic stop in Houston on July 7. The Department of Homeland Security says Salgado Araujo was not the person agents were looking for.</p><p>Mexico President Claudia Sheinbaum has referred to these deaths as “homicides.” As she called for more accountability at a news conference announcing steps her government was taking, Sheinbaum said Mexico “cannot turn a blind eye to the Mexicans who have died.</p><p>“We are going to do everything within our power,” Sheinbaum said. “What we cannot do is stand by as Mexicans die in ICE operations or detention.”</p><p>Mexico’s effort has three tracks. Mexico has filed criminal complaints with state and county prosecutors in Illinois and elsewhere, and it plans to submit a complaint to the U.S. Department of Justice, seeking independent investigations into the deaths. The Mexican government also issued cease- and-desist letters directing U.S. detention centers to preserve records and called for a formal review by the United Nations Human Rights Council.</p><p>It will be up to U.S. officials to decide whether to investigate or file charges.</p><p>Legal experts and immigration advocates say it’s unclear whether U.S. authorities will cooperate with an investigation but that the process still could put political pressure on the United States to take action and potentially yield evidence that could be used for civil lawsuits.</p><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Can Mexico force the U.S. to investigate?</h3><p>Mexico can’t compel the United States to investigate or collect evidence, experts say.</p><p>Mexico already is encountering resistance from U.S. officials. Earlier this week, Mexico said the State Department returned a cease-and-desist letter it sent regarding four Mexican citizens who died earlier this year at the Adelanto detention center in San Bernardino County.</p><p>For any sort of investigation into individual deaths, U.S. prosecutors could determine whether there is a basis to investigate, decline to open an investigation or later decide not to file charges in any of these cases, says <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/08/15/cartels-chapo-elchapo-ilan-katz-claudia-sheinbaum-sinaloa-cartel" target="_blank" ><u>Ilan Katz,</u></a> a Mexico-based criminal defense lawyer who is president of the Mexican Bar Foundation.</p><p>“When a government goes to the Department of Justice, it is like any person going to the DOJ," Katz says. "The department has the discretion to act or not act, but it has now been informed of alleged criminal conduct."</p><p>He says he can’t predict what will happen this time.</p><p>“We don’t know, especially because, in the world of Trump, [the] DOJ has become — or at least seems to have become — less independent than it was in the past,” Katz says.</p><p>Tom Ginsburg, a University of Chicago law professor who focuses on constitutional and international law, says that, even though the Mexican government can’t force the United States to investigate, it can send an important political message tol Mexican citizens that their government “ is not abandoning them.”</p><p>But he says international law can do little to force the United States to take accountability.</p><p>“In general, there’s your rights, and then there’s what are the remedies,” he says. “What’s the mechanism for enforcing it?”</p><p>He says there are few ways to compel a country to remedy a violation of international law, and the United States has often resisted complying.</p><p>“I know no one’s holding their breath with the Trump administration,” he says.</p><div class="Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has called for more accountablity for the deaths of 17 Mexican nationals who dies in ICE custody or during other ICE operations.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>AP Photo/Marco Ugarte</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Waiting for answers</h3><p>Villegas González’s case shows what those limits mean for a family and a community.</p><p>Reyna Torres Mendívil, Mexico’s consul general in Chicago, says Mexico first called for an investigation by the FBI on Sept. 13, 2025, a day after Villegas González died. It also sent a diplomatic request to the U.S. Embassy in Mexico.</p><p>In a statement, a spokesperson for DHS says the “ criminal prosecution of the involved ICE officer was declined by the United States Attorney's Office,” but pursuant to ICE policy, “the ICE Office of Professional Responsibility is continuing its administrative review of the incident.“</p><p>In May, the Illinois State Police <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/05/ice-midway-blitz-chicago-trump-silverio-villegas-gonzalez" target="_blank" ><u>said it had opened</u></a> an investigation into the death of Villegas González. No results have been made public.</p><p>Torres Mendívil said attorneys representing the Villegas family are conducting their own inquiry as they consider possible legal action. “They are carrying out a parallel investigation into the circumstances and everything that happened, for whatever legal action may be appropriate,” Torres Mendívil says.</p><p>The consulate did not answer subsequent questions seeking specifics about whether the family has taken legal action into the death of Villegas González.</p><p>The consulate cannot represent families directly in U.S. courts, but Torres Mendívil said it can provide money for outside lawyers on a case-by-case basis. “We do provide resources so that attorneys can do it,” she said. “Not in every case. The case has to be viable.”</p><p>In Villegas González’s case, she said the consulate is “assisting the family with the payment of the attorneys” working to reunify his children with relatives.</p><h3><b>Building a record and pressure</b></h3><p>Mexico has also made a formal request to the United Nation to gather information about the deaths, including that of Villegas González, and examine whether the United States met its duties under international law.</p><p>The U.N. could ask U.S. officials what happened, review whether the deaths were properly investigated and call for more information, further investigation or changes in U.S. practices.</p><p>Sarah Dávila, an associate professor of law at UIC and director of the International Human Rights Clinic who says she was speaking on behalf of herself and not the university, says the United States has a duty under international human-rights law to investigate reports of abuse. But the U.N. Human Rights Council cannot force U.S. agencies to comply.</p><p>“While recommendations from the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights are not binding, or findings from United Nations procedures, they carry enormous weight,” Dávila says.</p><p>She says those findings could create an independent record and later be used in civil or criminal cases in the U.S.</p><p>The cease-and-desist letters do not carry legal force on their own but serve as a formal “warning” not to destroy or alter evidence and can become important if a case later goes to trial, experts say.</p><p>Ginsburg says Mexico could also make a case before the U.N. that the rights of its citizens were violated under international law. That could include violations of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, which requires the agency detaining a foreign national to allow the detainee to have access to their consular officials, who could visit them in detention and help them obtain a lawyer.</p><p>According to Shaw Drake, an assistant professor at the University of New Mexico School of Law, Mexico could have another source of leverage. The United States relies heavily on Mexico to accept deportees, including people from countries other than Mexico.</p><p>“If Mexico refuses to receive those third-country nationals [for deportation], it puts a major wrench in the administration’s current mass deportation efforts,” Drake says.</p><p>This could give Mexico’s demands for accountability greater political weight, he said, if the country chooses to use it.</p><p>Artemio Arreola, political director of the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights says that even though he thinks Mexico’s announcement is mainly political and diplomatic, investigations are still important because families deserve to know exactly how their relatives died, particularly when evidence has contradicted official accounts.</p><p>“These investigations are even more important because, in many of these cases, the official accounts have turned out to be false,” he says.</p><p>“Authorities have put forward narratives that later evidence has contradicted. “We have to know exactly how these deaths occurred.”<br></p>

entries.title: Jury convicts three in robbery spree that targeted Irish Nobleman Pub, liquor and convenience stores
entries.summary: <p>Three<b> </b>men<b> </b>face significant prison sentences<b> </b>after<b> </b>a<b> </b>federal<b> </b>jury<b> </b>convicted<b> </b>them<b> </b>Tuesday<b> </b>for<b> </b>their roles in a series<b> </b>of<b> </b>violent<b> </b>armed<b> </b>robberies<b> </b>of<b> </b>Chicago<b> </b>liquor stores, convenience stores and bars<b> </b>that netted them nearly<b> </b>$300,000.</p><p>Ardaries Harris, 28; Jordan Fox, 26;<b> </b>and<b> </b>Xavier<b> </b>Harris, 27, are already in federal custody on robbery conspiracy charges, records show. The jury convicted them on nearly every count in a 23-count indictment, according to U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’ office.</p><p>The verdict followed a lengthy trial in the courtroom of U.S. District Judge Andrea Wood.</p><p>A fourth defendant, Roosevelt<b> </b>Veal, is set to face trial separately, records show.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Lofton is now deceased.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>U.S. District Court records</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The robbery spree lasted from August 2023, starting with the robbery of Ace’s Liquor and Tap in the 4400 block of West Armitage, and continued for nine months until the May 2024<b> </b>attempted robbery of Basil Food & Liquor<b> </b>in the 7400 block<b> </b>of North Western.</p><p>It included the May 2024<b> </b>robbery<b> </b>of the Irish Nobleman Pub<b> </b>in West Town, records show. That early morning robbery began when Fox, Ardaries Harris and Veal ran inside, with Fox pointing a Glock pistol modified with a switch at people in the pub, according to prosecutors.</p><p>The switch turned the gun<b> </b>into a fully automatic firearm<b> </b>that could fire multiple bullets<b> </b>at the pull of a trigger.</p><p>“Hands up, hands up,” Fox<b> </b>told people inside the bar, according to the feds. “Come here, everybody come here before I drop the switch. Come here. Fully automatic. Come on.”</p><p>The owner of the bar ran across the street to his house to call 911, records show. Fox fired at him but missed,<b> </b>as Fox and the others fled, prosecutors said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>U.S. District Court records</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In a video recorded<b> </b>after<b> </b>another series of robberies days later, prosecutors said the men could be seen counting cash<b> </b>with<b> </b>a<b> </b>stolen<b> </b>bottle<b> </b>of<b> </b>Don Julio<b> </b>tequila nearby. In another, Ardaries Harris drank from the tequila bottle, displayed piles of cash and said, “I’m stackin’ this s--- all summer and all winter.”</p><p>Defense attorneys for the three defendants did not immediately comment. Prosecutors have said the case was built with help from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2023/9/27/23891321/chicago-crime-guns-atf" target="_blank" >Crime Gun Intelligence Center</a>.</p><p>Assistant U.S. attorneys Emily<b> </b>Vermylen, Stephanie<b> </b>Stern<b> </b>and<b> </b>Jalan<b> </b>Jaskot outlined the details of the case, as well as the robbery crew’s pattern, in a court filing<b> </b>in April. The<b> </b>robberies<b> </b>all<b> </b>occurred at night, they said. The robbers operated in groups of two to four and would enter the businesses<b> </b>with guns drawn.</p><p>Fox would typically approach the cash register<b> </b>with a bag and gun, the prosecutors said.<b> </b>He would either steal<b> </b>from the register<b> </b>or take “overflow money”<b> </b>stored nearby. Other members of the robbery crew would<b> </b>“take control”<b> </b>of patrons<b> </b>and employees<b> </b>at gunpoint, robbing them of cash<b> </b>and<b> </b>taking<b> </b>their cell phones.</p><p>“The defendants — disguised by dark-colored hoods, gloves, and masks — terrorized employees and customers by holding them up at gunpoint; frequently beating them, including with firearms; and in four instances, shooting at employees,” the feds wrote.</p>
